title: Clo Test By @Garretttrenholm
description: clo3d #digitalfashion #fashiondesigner.
transcript:
This past week, I wanted to see how
accurate Clo 3D renders were when it
came to making actual physical garments.
After putting in my measurements and
making a design I was happy with, I
printed out the pattern and sewed a
sample together without making pretty
much any alterations to the digital
pattern. It turned out pretty much close
to a good copy for the very first
sample. And so far, I think I'm going to
be using CL 3D a lot in the future.
summary: # Clo Test by @Garretttrenholm ## Introduction This past week, I wanted to see how accurate Clo 3D renders were when it came to making actual physical garments. ## Design Process After putting in my measurements and making a design I was happy with, I printed out the pattern and sewed a sample together without making pretty much any alterations to the digital pattern. ## Results It turned out pretty much close to a good copy for the very first sample. ## Future Use So far, I think I'm going to be using Clo 3D a lot in the future.

summary: # Clo User Story - MAS ## Introduction to MAS MAS is a $2 billion global leader in apparel technology, collaborating with some of the most iconic fashion brands to bring ideas from concept to market. At the heart of MAS are four core values: innovation, sustainability, co-creation, and collaboration. ## The Role of Clo Clo is an essential building block that helps MAS reimagine product development. It brings speed and precision to every stage across different business units. Let's take a closer look at how the MAS and Clo partnership is bringing this vision to life. ## Product Creation Process At MAS, product creation begins with research and ideation. This involves diving into consumer insights, trends, and market data to understand industry needs and identify gaps in the market. Our focus is on consumer-centric innovation, delivering commercially viable products of superior craftsmanship. ### Concepting, Design, and Development From the foundation of research, we move into concepting, design, and development. We leverage key tools in our digital toolkit, including Clo with its 3D capabilities and generative features. This seamless workflow enables us to take ideas from concept to prototype with precision and agility, aiding in digital visualization and ensuring our first physical samples are accurate. ## Collaboration and Co-Creation Collaboration starts long before a garment is stitched. MAS functions as a center for product design and innovation for our customers. Co-creation is a cycle that begins before the season, continues throughout, and even extends after the season ends, facilitating genuine product collaboration. With 3D serving as a universal language for creatives, Clo and its suite of tools support our end-to-end workflows, enabling connectivity and creative exchange throughout the calendar. This approach contributes to making informed product decisions in collaboration with our customers. ## Material Development at MAS In the Digital Product Creation (DPC) process, material development is where everything begins. A centralized sampling unit has captured over 4,000 fabrics in just two years, supporting more than 50 global brands by capturing texture, stretch, and drape. We create authentic digital twins that bring consistency and precision to every stage of development, setting new standards for fabric realism. ## Innovations in Digital Lace At MAS, we have been reimagining how lace and warp knits are developed and visualized. Since starting our digital lace journey in 2021, we have made significant progress with the support of tools like Clo. The impact is evident; with our connected ecosystem of tools, we have made digital sampling over 40% faster. These gains in speed and accuracy are enhancing our agility and reliability as a partner in DPC. ## Advancements in Knitting Technology Leading the way in advanced knitting, MAS combines engineered and circular knitting to push the boundaries of what's possible. We were among the first vendors to enable a fully seamless digital product creation workflow, providing our customers with a faster, more accurate, and flexible development process. While seamless garment construction has historically been complex and costly, digital product creation is helping us reduce lead times, cut costs, and minimize waste. By pairing our knitting expertise with advanced tools like Clo and other platforms, we are innovating a smarter, more efficient, and sustainable approach for the industry. ## Creating True-to-Life Digital Twins To replicate true-to-life digital twins, we mimic graphic techniques digitally, such as heat seal, foil, and embroidery. These detailed textures are imported into Clo, where artwork and patterns are graded, ensuring precision and reducing errors in the sampling stage. We fully utilize Clo’s specialized tools to create accurate digital twins, from pressure and stress maps that enhance visual accuracy to building inclusive size sets and evaluating fit across diverse size ranges. Although digital garment fit remains a challenge across the industry, we continuously explore new approaches and push the boundaries of what's possible in digital product creation. ## Transforming Digital Color Sampling At MAS, digital color sampling has revolutionized our workflow, enabling us and our partners to review prints and colorways faster, even with complex fabrics. Clo is one of the platforms we use within this workflow, functioning as a collaborative workspace where we utilize real-time comments and annotations to streamline feedback and reduce approval cycles. By reviewing designs directly on the platform, decision-making is expedited, allowing us to remain responsive to changes. ## Conclusion: The Future of Digital Product Creation At MAS, digital product creation transcends being merely a process; it embodies how we bring innovation, creativity, and collaboration to life. We have evolved from building foundational processes to creating future-ready models that enable us and our partners to work smarter. With trusted partners like Clo, we are redefining how fashion is created digitally. As 3D and AI technologies continue to evolve, we stand at the forefront of a new era—one that challenges us not only to create faster but also to create with greater meaning. Together, we are not just shaping the future of fashion; we are shaping the future of possibility.

summary: # How To Organize Your Clo Projects And Collaborate In Clo-Set ## Introduction Hello! In this video, we would like to share a quick overview of features in our platform, Closet, that are especially useful for freelancers and hobbyists using CL. ## What is Closet? Closet is something like a CL cloud. It functions like Dropbox or Drive for all your CL projects, whether they are project files themselves or 3D garments. It also supports digitized fabrics, 3D trims, avatars, and more. You can manage your 3D assets anytime from anywhere and collaborate with others, sharing feedback in real-time. Use it as a library for communication, garment presentation, and to organize collections. ## Workspace Overview From your workspace, you can see all the content within your virtual closet, as well as visual boards. Within rendering, you can view information about renders performed in the cloud. We will get back to both topics in a bit. ## Default Closet Structure There is a default closet structure for you to store your files, but it can be reorganized and renamed within the general framework called groups. You can create companies, and within those companies, brands and workrooms. This way, you can organize your collections and clients in separate spaces. I have created a structure here containing a demo brand within a demo company. The collection we are looking at right now is organized in a workroom called "Denim." ## Style Page Features If you upload a project to Closet, a style page is created with the following options: - **Style Info:** On the left, you will find style info such as date, creator, status, and notification options. - **File Management:** You can upload and download versions of the project or garment file, generate tech packs, and access the render settings of the file. - **File History:** Through the file history, you can track the evolution of a style and go back to a previous version if necessary, for example, by uploading your updates to a file at the end of every day. In the middle, you see the 3D viewport with a turntable preview where you can annotate and switch between colorways. You can create annotations by clicking on the top right button, "Comment" or "Draw," and then press "Complete." ## Comments and Annotations Within the right column, you will find a list of all comments and annotations left on the style, as well as colorways, attachments, and information on whom the style has been shared with. ## Access Control Everything you add on Closet is protected and only viewable by those to whom you have granted access. As the administrator and creator of the structure, you can edit and delete anything within it. You can invite others as either editors or viewers. Editors can upload and download the files they have access to, while viewers can only view but not edit. ## Rendering Functionality In addition to storage, the platform also provides a rendering function via the Closet server, so you don't have to do it on your own computer. This is especially useful if your hardware does not have high specs or if you want to render without occupying your CL license, allowing you to work on something else. Meanwhile, any renders that you have created via the Closet service will be accessible on the style page. ## Visual Boards As you can see on this project files viewport, outside of our workroom and style pages, you can access the visual board section from your dashboard. Here you can create virtual mood boards and showcase your designs using 3D assets directly pulled from Closet. This removes the need for other visual workspaces and portfolio creation tools. The final slides can contain interactive links connected to your assets. Simply drag and drop your components from the content browser on the right, change the colors of the background, add additional shapes, and add text, and so on. ## Efficient Collection Management As you categorize and work on your collections, you can filter through your workrooms and entire library quickly. For example, get an overview of all styles you have marked to adopt into the final lineup of your collection or filter by categories such as specific product groups. You can also search through the tags you have given to your styles. ## Additional Resources If you're looking for more info on Closet and the many more functions within it that we have not covered here, please check out our in-depth tutorials and skill apps, which can be found on the CL YouTube channel. As always, thank you for tuning in! Bye!

summary: # Enfants Riches Déprimés Leather Jacket By Sam Zona ## Introduction In this video, I explore the process of creating a working digital replica of a striking leather jacket. This journey involves reverse engineering a garment that presents both a challenge and an opportunity for creativity. ## Research and Inspiration The first step of my project was to conduct thorough research. I always aim to find the earliest reference piece available. However, I discovered that there are very few original garments of this type. Most designs are based on early military pieces or similar styles, particularly with jackets. ### Keyword Searching I engaged in extensive keyword searching, focusing on terms like "double-breasted moto jacket" and "double-breasted military button jacket." This research led me to two notable leather motorcycle jackets: the **Leather Toggs Backet** and the **Buco J31**. Both jackets date back to the 1940s and draw inspiration from World War I-era aviator jackets and police short double-breasted purpose-built leather jackets. ## Detailed Analysis Having access to more detailed images of these jackets significantly informed my construction process. The past clips shown on screen depict my efforts in arranging the pattern pieces and sewing them together. ### Construction Process After several simulations, I was pleased with how everything was coming together. At this stage, I was working on adding the final collar piece. Following this, I could move on to the intricate details, which included a multitude of zippers. #### Zipper Specifications One of the challenges I faced was that there is no way to save zipper settings for application in different areas. Each zipper must be customized individually, considering factors like teeth size, material, color, and tape length. This meticulous process is honestly one of my least favorite tasks in the project. ## Conclusion Overall, I feel that I have successfully replicated the essence of the original jacket. It looks quite close to the reference piece I was inspired by. I welcome feedback on my work and am eager to hear what you would like to see in the next video.

Go to **Assembly** and download the **Texture Source**. 2. Create the full rig by selecting **Assembly** and changing to **DCC Export**. This is important when we want to import the DNA file to Clo 3D. 3. Select your output folder and click **Assembly** again. 4. Save the DNA file for Clo 3D. ## Step 3: Importing the DNA File into Clo 3D Open Clo 3D. Go to **File** > **Import** > **DNA** and locate your folder. First, select the body file, then locate the head. After selecting, click **OK**. This will import your Metahuman body. ### Adding the Garment 1. Add the garment: first the skirt, then the turtleneck, and fit it to the character. 2. Open the **UV Editor** and use the **Out UV Packing Tool** to create a UV map. 3. Export your file as a USD file. ### Export Settings For the export settings, select: - **Include Garment** - **Select All Patterns** - **Single Object** - **Select Fig** - **Unified UV Coordinates** Ensure you select all of the maps you want to export, and include **Gin Simulation Data**. Then, go back to Unreal Engine. ## Step 4: Creating a Resizable Metahuman Wardrobe Asset Open your content browser. In the content browser in **Meshes**, you can always find your Metahum. Here, you will have all the Metahuman assets stored. Later on, you will import the combined skeletal mesh here. ### Organizing Folders 1. Create an **Outfits** folder: right-click and create a new folder. 2. Inside the **Outfits** folder, create another folder with the name of your asset (e.g., **D1**). 3. Go inside this folder and import the USD file. The import will automatically create another **Style 1** folder. This is important for later stages when you want to package your asset for the FAP marketplace. ### Folder Structure In this case, you need two folders with the exact same name: **Style 1** inside of **Style 1**. The USD import will create three subfolders within the style folder. You will mostly work in the **Static Meshes** to create your cloth asset later on. ## Step 5: Exporting the Combined Skeletal Mesh Go back to the meshes and select the Metahuman to export the combined skeletal mesh. Click on **Metahuman Character Export Outfit Body Skeleton Mesh** and then locate it in the Metahuman folder. Select the **Meshes** folder and save it. Now, close the Metahuman editor. You should see the combined skeletal mesh, which you will need for the cloth asset. ## Step 6: Creating the Physics Cloth Asset Go back to the working folder. In the **Static Meshes**, right-click and select **Physics Cloth Asset**. Name it something recognizable. This will also create a data flow node. ### Data Flow Node Configuration 1. Right-click on the CA node and select **Open** and **Data Flow Editor (Experimental)**. 2. Clear out all the unnecessary elements and insert your assets. 3. Delete everything besides the **Transfer Skin Weights**, **Remesh Nodes**, and **Cloth Asset Terminal Nodes**. ### Adding Nodes - Right-click and search for **Static Mesh Import** to add a static mesh import node. - Right-click again and search for **Remesh Node**. On the right side in the node details, select the static mesh **Style 1** of the outfit or choose it from the drop-down. Uncheck the **Import Simulation Mesh** checkbox since you don't have one. ### Connecting Nodes 1. Connect the **Static Mesh Import** to the collection on the **Transfer Skin Weights** node. 2. Connect the **Transfer Skin Weights** collection node to the **Cloth Asset Terminal Node**. 3. Connect the **Transfer Skin Weights** collection to the **Remesh Collection** and the **Remesh Collection** to **Collection LOD1**. In the construction viewport on the top, you can now see your asset. If you want to see the render view, select it on the right top. Save your project and go back to the content browser. ## Step 7: Finalizing the Outfit Asset Navigate to your main folder. Ensure it contains only your working folder and no other assets or folders. Right-click, select **Physics**, and select **Outfit Asset**. Name this outfit asset **Style 1 in Michaels** and select **Resizable Outfit**. Move the DF node to the working folder so you only have your outfit asset in the main folder. Open it by double-clicking. ### Data Flow Graph Evaluation In the top right corner, click the three dots next to **Evaluate Data Flow Graph**. Select **Manual Graph Evaluator** to avoid long processes during setup. In the **Data Flow Members** panel on the bottom left, check **Sized Outfit Source** and click the plus sign once for each cloth asset you have (in this case, only one). For each entry, select the source asset (our CA **Style 1**) and the source body parts (in this case, **Character 1 Combined Skeletal Mesh**). If you have more sizes, add them here. Click on **Evaluate Data Flow Graph**, and once done, turn automatic evaluation back on. Save it and close this window. ## Step 8: Testing the Outfit Asset To try this outfit asset on a new Metahuman, go back to your content folder into the meshes. Right-click and create a new Metahuman, naming it something like **Character 2**. Double-click to open this new Metahuman. ### Applying the Outfit Asset 1. Open the **Hair and Clothing** tab. 2. Scroll all the way down to the **Cloth Tab**. 3. Click on the current asset and remove it. To add your outfit asset from the content browser, go to your **Outfit** folder and drag and drop it to the current outfit tab. ### Verifying the Changes If you double-click now, you should see the outfit asset on your new Metahuman. If you go now to the body and change the size, you can see that the clothing is changing with the body. Finally, close the Metahuman editor, and you will see your wardrobe asset also in the content browser.

Everyone keeps asking me, "What app is
that?" And it's not an app. It's called
Clothe 3D. It's like Illustrator on
steroids. Instead of flat sketches, you
build real garments starting with base
patterns on true to size avatars. Why is
this better? You can test the fabric,
the cut, the drape, the fit, the trims,
and the colors, all before you even make
a sample. That alone can cut months off
your development timeline. And factories
love it because there's less guesswork.
And the wild part, you can export the
patterns, sew the pieces together with
around 90% accuracy. If you're designing
clothes in 2025 without CL, you're
getting left behind.
summary: # What Is Clo By Tim Last ## Introduction to Clo 3D Everyone keeps asking me, "What app is that?" And it's not an app. It's called Clo 3D. ## Overview of Clo 3D Clo 3D is like Illustrator on steroids. Instead of flat sketches, you build real garments starting with base patterns on true-to-size avatars. ## Advantages of Using Clo 3D ### Testing Features Why is this better? You can test the fabric, the cut, the drape, the fit, the trims, and the colors—all before you even make a sample. ### Efficiency in Development That alone can cut months off your development timeline. Factories love it because there's less guesswork involved in the process. ## Exporting Patterns The wild part is that you can export the patterns and sew the pieces together with around 90% accuracy. ## Conclusion If you're designing clothes in 2025 without Clo 3D, you're getting left behind.

These webinars take you through the step-by-step process to help you optimize your flow pipeline. Let's start with quick introductions. I am Nam, VP of Business Development for the Indian Subcontinent and Southwest Asia. - **Raj**: I'm a Design and Implementation Specialist at Clo India office. - **Arya**: Designer Implementation Specialist at Clo India office. Today, we come together for the third webinar titled "Fit Proto: Refine and Review" of our End to End Clo Virtual Series. ## Overview of the Webinar Series The End to End Clo Virtual Series is aimed at optimizing your entire 3D product development process, incorporating exciting new Clo features, and following the industry workflow. If you've been following the series, you will know that we have covered the Digital Asset Library in our first webinar, followed by Design Proto. The third one today is all about Fit Proto, and upcoming topics will cover production and taking a step further to marketing and e-commerce. For those who have missed out or want to rewatch any of the past webinars in the series, you can find the link in the description. ## Webinar Content Let's talk about the content for this webinar. We will start by taking a Design Proto and then make it fit-ready by checking the avatars, fabrics, doing realistic construction, and much more. These aspects are essential when making a file fit-ready. ### Transition to Fit Proto Right now, you may be wondering what a Fit Proto is or what the difference is between Design Proto and Fit Proto. We already made our Design Proto; now why do we need to create a Fit Proto? The main difference is that with Design Proto, our agenda is to check the aesthetics of the garment. You want to check the color of the garment, conceptualize it in different colors and prints, check the scale of your print, the size of your graphics, and their placement. All of these important aesthetic decisions can be made using a Design Proto. Once your design and range are finalized, the Fit Proto allows you to check the functional validation. You can ensure that the garment is not too tight or too loose, check the levels and length of the garment, and see if it fits every size set properly. All of these crucial decisions can be made using a Fit Proto. ### Importance of Fit Proto The reason you need to differentiate between Design Proto and Fit Proto is that at the design stage, you do not want to include excessive technical information as many files might get rejected. Therefore, putting in all that hard work and resources at the Design Proto stage can be a waste of time. Once your design and range are finalized, you can refine those selected designs into a Fit Proto to check the fit of the garment. With a Fit Proto, you can eliminate the need for physical samples and virtually check the fit of your garment in Clo. It also enables real-time collaborations because different teams with their own expertise can participate and contribute insights to the sample you are creating in Clo. This reduces risks in production by identifying key challenges or issues that could have arisen with your virtual sample in Clo. ### Metaphor of Fit To give you an idea about the fit of a garment, let's compare it to the fit of a person. Just as our health depends on exercise, diet, stress, and sleep, the fit of a 3D file depends on how accurate your avatar is, the correct fabric, realistic construction, high-resolution simulation, and the post-production processes. We will discuss all of this in detail in the next few slides. ## Avatar Size Let's go ahead and first talk about the correct avatar size. In Clo, avatars or dummies have a huge impact on the fit of your garment. You have two key attributes of the avatar that play a significant role: the avatar size and the avatar shape. Both of these are crucial when discussing the correct dummy size. In Clo, we have an avatar editor that helps you customize the shape and size of the Clo avatars. We have already covered this in our first webinar in detail. If you want to do a revision or watch it again, you can click on the link in the description. We also have auto-convert to avatar, which takes any of your 3D scanned bodies or OBJ files and converts them to a Clo-compatible avatar. It automatically matches all the measurements and the shape based on your 3D scan file. ### External Avatars We are compatible with external avatars such as Humanics, Alvinon, and Meshcaped. If you are working with any of those, you can bring them directly to Clo for your fitting rounds. Additionally, with our 2025.2 update, you can also bring your Metahumans DNA into Clo and use them for fittings. ### General Rules for Avatar Usage When working with avatars, keep the following rules in mind: - Never use the generic preset Clo avatar for the fitting stage. - Auto-convert your physical dummies or models or use the Clo avatar editor to create your own avatars that replicate the size of your physical dummies or models. - Bring in external digital avatars if applicable. - If you are working with a brand, use the avatars provided by that brand. ## Fabrics Now let's talk about fabrics, as this is another critical factor that dictates the fit of your particular style. We have covered a lot about this in our first webinar. We have our defaults library with lots of fabrics, and you can also purchase or download fabrics created by our users. We also have our AI Fabric Creator, where you can input the composition and weight of your fabric, and the AI will create the digital fabric for you. Additionally, we have our Fabric Digitization Service. ### Fabric Properties When discussing fabric properties, there are two important key points: visual properties and physical properties. The physical properties, including weight, thickness, stretch, and bend of the fabric, are much more important than the visual properties when doing fittings in Clo. To measure the physical properties, we have our ZFAB kit, which is an automatic fabric kit set to launch next year. You can cut a swatch of your fabric and use this machine to automatically digitize and measure all physical properties of your fabric. ### Visual Properties While visual properties are not as crucial for fit, they can affect how the garment drapes and how the fit is perceived. This will be discussed further in the digital-physical comparison section of this webinar. It is important to validate your digital fabrics regularly to ensure that your physical fabric matches the Clo fabric. If you are working for a brand, use only the fabrics provided by that brand. ## Realistic Construction Next, let's discuss realistic construction. Certain areas of the garment need to be replicated in Clo to achieve the right fit. For seams, we know that in Clo, we sew based on the sewing line, not the cutting line. You can either replicate the seam as it is in Clo or replicate the properties of the seam. ### Practical Examples For example, you may want to create a self-fold hem or apply tension to a seam that does not stretch. The idea is to replicate the same construction in Clo to achieve accurate fitting. In today's session, we will refine a t-shirt, a shirt, activewear, and denim to make them fit-ready by adding realistic construction. ### T-shirt Refinement For the t-shirt, we will refine the sleeve first. We will create a self-fold hem by offsetting the pattern outline. This extra extension will add weight to your garment, changing the fall. The same process will be applied to the bottom hem of the shirt and the neckband. We will also apply a steam tool to replicate the steaming process used in real life, ensuring that the neckband lies flat. ### Shirt Refinement For the shirt, we will ensure that the cuffs are double-layered, create a realistic placket construction, and ensure the collar has a proper double-layered finish. ### Denim Refinement For denim, we will focus on realistic construction for the zipper and the J flap, ensuring that the waistband is double-layered and creating realistic pocket constructions. ### Activewear Refinement For activewear, we will ensure that the top part is double-layered and apply elastic at 100% on the side seams to prevent them from stretching. ## Fitting Review Process Now that we've discussed realistic construction, let's move on to the fitting review process. This involves a quality checklist, garment fit maps, and a suggested workflow for fit checking. ### 3D File Quality Checklist When reviewing a 3D fit sample, make sure to check: - 2D pattern alignment with the physical sample. - Avatar measurements and poses. - Correct sewing and fold arrangements. - Stable simulations, especially with multi-layered patterns. - High-resolution properties for accurate drape and stretch. ### Garment Fit Maps Understanding fit maps is crucial. The stress map, strain map, fit map, and pressure map provide insights into how the garment interacts with the avatar and identifies areas for improvement. ### Suggested Workflow For analyzing these maps: 1. Customize the strain map according to the fabric’s stretch capacity. 2. Analyze the stress and pressure maps to assess tightness or looseness. 3. Use the strain map to determine how stretchy the fabric is, ensuring all values are aligned with the physical fabric. ## Case Study with Industry Partner We had an exclusive interview with Shriram from Aquarel India, who shared insights from their experience with the fitting workflow using Clo. summary: # Get Started With CLO! Beginner's Quick Start Guide ## Introduction Hey everyone! [music] My name is Ariel, and we are going to be going over a CLO quick start guide in today's video. Now, if you're curious, this is a re-recording of our CLO live session from October. Due to some of the quality not being the best, we decided it would be a good idea to record this and put it on our YouTube as a regular tutorial so you guys would have the best quality version of the video. As I said, my name is Ariel. I'm a 3D designer and CX manager here at CLO in our New York City office. In this video, we will cover everything you need to get started using CLO. We will discuss: - How to download assets from our Connect platform. - Importing an avatar and pattern. - Arranging the pattern, sewing it, and applying fabrics, prints, colors, and graphics. - Finally, we will end with a nice render. I hope you enjoy this video today and learn a little (or a lot) about CLO and really how to get started using it. ## Downloading Assets from Connect Let's start with how to actually download what we need to use besides CLO, and that will be downloaded from our Connect store right here. We recently created a CLO Designer YouTube live channel with our friendly little Clonion. You will see here the "Intro to CLO Dress" from October 10th. To download, click on the shopping cart icon, which will instantly add the item to your cart. If you want to look further into it, you can click on the thumbnail for a more in-depth view. As you scroll down, you will see that it came from a design source from our Connect Store. You can activate a 3D viewer to see the full 3D built style as well as some additional attachments that this comes with. We will want our DXF or pattern file, a PNG for some textures, a tag to add, and a fun little graphic. I’m going to go ahead and add to cart. Now I can see in the upper right corner a little number one next to my cart. Perfect! It’s been added there for me. Once in my cart section, I’m ready to check out. Pay attention: this is a free asset for you guys to use. The total shows zero, so I just have to agree to the Connect terms of service and click "Place Order." Once I place the order, CLO will automatically take me to my purchase tab. Within the purchase tab, I can click the checkbox or just download the item that I want. I want to download this asset to use in CLO. ## Unzipping the Downloaded Folder After downloading, you’ll see that there is a folder that has been downloaded. It is currently a zip folder, as indicated by the zipper across the folder thumbnail. An important point is that a zipped folder cannot be linked into CLO, so we need to unzip this. On a PC, I’ll click on the folder and select "Extract All." I’ll extract this right into my downloads folder, which is completely fine. After extraction, I see another folder that has been created. If I click in, I can see everything that comes into that folder, including the DXF pattern, graphics, a tag, and a clip project file for reference. ## Launching CLO Now that we have our files downloaded, let's jump into CLO. I have CLO launched on my monitor and I’m on version 2025.1.240. We can always check the version by looking in the lower left corner. One major change to note is that if you are looking at older CLO tutorials, you might see the word "Library" on the left-hand side. As of 2025, the CLO library was updated and moved to a linked icon in the upper right corner. We will cover the library in a moment, but just in case you're looking at an old tutorial, now you know where to find it! ## User Interface Overview Let’s talk about what we see on the screen. On the left side, we have our **3D window**, where our avatar will live and where our garment will be once it’s all sewn together. On the left side, we also have our **3D toolbar** and a vertical toggle to turn visuals on or off. If you want to learn more about vertical toggles, there is a tutorial on our CLO YouTube channel. On the 2D side, this is where our pattern will live, like a pattern cutting table. We have another vertical toggle for the 2D window, providing more or less information based on what we choose to turn on or off. The **object browser** on the right side is like our bill of materials, housing items like fabrics, graphics, buttons, buttonholes, and topstitching. Currently, I’m in my fabric tab, so I see only fabric 1. Below that, we have our **property editor**, which will populate with information about whatever I select. ## User Settings What if your user interface looks a little different than mine? That’s completely okay. To check everything, go to the top of your screen where it says “Settings,” then “User Settings.” In **user settings**, you can look at graphics options, view controls, shortcuts, user interface preferences, unit systems, and more. I will be using inches, which is common in the US. If you're more comfortable with centimeters or millimeters, feel free to change it. You can also adjust decimal points for precision, and options for how buttons appear. ### Adjusting Graphics Settings For view controls, ensure you have a proper mouse setup. I’m using a three-button mouse, which is recommended. If you have a different mouse, like a Magic Mouse, just note that your commands might differ slightly. You can also customize shortcuts if you want to personalize them in the future. ## Accessing the CLO Library Where do we start when we're ready to work on a project and have a pattern to use? We will access the CLO library. Hovering over the CLO library, you’ll see a dropdown with the name of the tool and the shortcut, which is “Y.” Opening the CLO library, we see three main tabs: the CLO tab with default assets, the CLO set tab for cloud assets, and the Connect tab for our downloaded assets. ### Linking Folders in the Library I already have CLO live linked, but let’s start from scratch and link the folder we want to use for CLO. Most likely, your folder is in your downloads. I recommend creating a folder directly on your desktop, calling it "CLO Live" or "CLO Tutorials," to prevent losing things in your downloads. To link a new folder, click the plus icon and choose "Create New Library." This will open a window to add a folder. I’ll select the folder I want and click "Select Folder." Now, I have a new tab added with all the assets. You can label these folders for easier access, and link in your personal folders with prints, graphics, and patterns. ## Importing Patterns Let’s add our CLO01 dress pattern. Right-click and choose "Add to Workspace." This will open the add DXF popup, where we have several options. The load type is set to “Add,” which means we will add this to whatever is currently in CLO. We can leave the autoscale option on, and the other default options are fine. I’ll click "OK." Now, we can see the patterns in both the 3D and 2D windows. Remember, these windows work in sync with one another. ## Adding an Avatar Before we start assembling our dress, we need an avatar or mannequin. Press "Y" on your keyboard to reopen the library. Go to the CLO tab, then the avatar tab. Inside the avatar tab, you’ll see options for baby, female, male, and more. Today, we'll use a mannequin. I’ll double-click the FV2.1 mannequin avatar and add it to the workspace. Now, I can see the avatar in my 3D space, as well as its shadow in the 2D space. ## Navigating the Scene Before we arrange our patterns, let’s talk about navigation—how to zoom, pan, and rotate in CLO. To zoom, use your scroll wheel. You can also click and hold the scroll wheel to pan. To rotate, hold the right click while dragging the mouse. If you find your view is off, pressing the number “2” on your keyboard will reset your view to front and center. ## Arranging Pattern Pieces Now we’ll arrange our pattern pieces. We will use the **Transform Pattern Tool** (shortcut A) to select and move our pattern pieces around. I recommend organizing your pattern pieces around the shadow of the avatar. For example, place the sleeve a bit off to the right and align the skirt patterns below the corresponding bodice pieces. Once arranged in the 2D window, we can reset the arrangement in the 3D window using the **Reset 2D Arrangement** button on the toolbar. ## Duplicating Pattern Pieces Now that we have half a dress, let’s duplicate the sleeve pattern. Right-click on the sleeve and choose "Clone Pattern with Linked Editing," then "Symmetric Pattern with Sewing" (shortcut D). This gives us a mirrored sleeve for the opposite side. summary: # Clo 2025.2 Feature Highlights ## Introduction Let's dive into the newest features of CL 2025.2. ## Knitwear Design Functionality First, we've expanded our knitwear design functionality within CL with our knit swatch editor. Select your knitwear fabric and click the yarn icon next to stitching. Here, you'll be able to design knit swatches with precision. Adjust your gauge size and yarn thickness and apply different stitch types. Then, simulate and apply it to the garment. Visualize different knit styles in seconds. ## Pattern Drafter Updates We've added more categories to our pattern drafter. Now you can easily draft both trousers and skirts. For trousers, we have two options: elastic waistband and slacks. You can create your pattern by entering simple measurements as shown here, or you can switch to general measurements, which allows you to input more details for increased control and precision. You can also draft trousers and skirts with our AI pattern drafter tool. For skirts, select between basic and flare options. Enter a text prompt, generate an image, and use that image to generate your pattern. Alternatively, you can upload any image and generate a pattern from that. ## Improved Fit Checking Now you can check the fit and edit garments even faster and more accurately than ever with soft body using GPU simulation. Simply switch to GPU simulation, turn on soft body, and watch how the fit changes. ## Notches and Grading We've updated our notches to be more precise for graded sizes. Now, when you turn on grading, you can see all of your notches across all of your graded sizes at once. You can control the placement of the notches for each size. ## Texture Editor Enhancements You can now make seamless repeats easier than ever. The new update to our texture editor lets you quickly and easily flip images horizontally, vertically, or even both. ## Graphic Measurements in Property Editor Our update to graphic measurements in the property editor allows you to move graphics by entering the exact position values. Place your graphics exactly where you want them. ## Zipper Duplication Now you can effortlessly duplicate zippers to symmetric patterns simply by right-clicking the zipper and selecting that option. Deactivating linked patterns also applies to zippers. ## Library Docking We heard that many of you want to be able to dock your library. So now you can click this arrow to move your library back to where it originally was. With this update, the old library will no longer be available in CL. ## Metahumans Integration Now you can easily design with Metahumans and CL. Import different bodies and heads in DNA file format for seamless integration with Unreal Engine and other platforms. Once you're done designing in CL, you can export everything back to the Metahuman creator. Your garment will automatically resize to any changes you make to the Metahuman's body, making it easier than ever to create high-quality realistic renders with Metahumans. ## Accessory Registration for Hats We're excited to announce that we've expanded the accessory registration feature to include hats in this release. Simply select your patterns or OPJs and register them as a hat. Once registered, you can add your hat to any of your projects. ## Avatar Customization for Kids We also know how much you value avatar customization within CL. So, we've expanded that to kid avatars. Change the avatar's hair, eyes, eyebrows, underwear, skin, and more, all within CL. ## Animation Tools and Key Frame Options We've added a few new user-friendly tools within animation along with more key frame options. Now, all layers can be easily added with the click of a button. We've also added the options for solidify, pattern shrinkage, and pressure. We've made it easy to add these key frames by allowing you to add multiple key frames at once using the option to apply key frames to all layers or selected layers. ## Conclusion Thank you guys so much for watching. We can't wait to see what you come up with using CL 2025.2. Have fun creating in CL!

summary: ```markdown # Learn How To Register As A Connect Seller With Kawany 👩‍🏫 ## Introduction Hi, everyone! I'm Kawany, CX Manager at CLO. Today, I'm going to walk you through the step-by-step process of how to sell an asset on CONNECT, our marketplace where users can share and sell their CLO and Marvelous creations. ## Step 1: Logging In First, log in to your CONNECT account. ## Step 2: Uploading Your Asset Now that you're logged in, click on "Upload" in the top right corner. Take a look at the types of files you can upload. ### Select the Store Option Next, select the “Store” option. Choose the asset file from your computer and upload it. ### Uploading the Thumbnail Now, upload the thumbnail for your file. If needed, you can access the manual to find more detailed recommendations for your image. ## Step 3: Asset Details Set a title, description, and tags for your asset. We suggest adding this in English to better reach international buyers. If your asset includes other elements, like separated accessories, you can also add additional images showing details and other points of view of the garment under the “Additional Images” section. ### Choosing a Category Next, we’ll select the category for our item. For my assets, I’ll select the “Women” category. I’ll also choose “T-shirt > Sweatshirt.” Here you can also select "Casual" or "Uniform." ## Step 4: Pricing and Publishing Now that we’ve added all the details of our asset, let's move to pricing and publishing. You can choose between two options: - **Free Item**: Simply finalize and publish; no further action is required. - **Paid Item**: This is our focus today. You need to set a price for your item. ### Design Source Price If your asset includes resources from another user, the “Design Source Price” field will appear with the proportional value already included. ### Extended License Price What is the extended license price? The Extended License Price is a special license charged when your asset is used for commercial purposes in 3D environments or by corporate users. This is why pricing is different for these users. ### Finalizing Your Asset After setting the price for your asset, you can save it as a draft or choose “Publish.” If you select “Publish,” your asset will go through a review and approval process before being published. Check the approval criteria for your asset at the link in the video description. All drafts are saved under the “Collection” tab in your portfolio. ## Step 5: Understanding Platform Fees Now, let's talk about platform fees. CONNECT takes a 30% commission on your profit. As a seller, you receive 70%, as long as the buyer is not located in the U.S. If the buyer is a U.S. resident, an additional tax will apply according to U.S. tax regulations. You can check the article in the video description to see the tax rate that applies to your region. We recommend considering these fees when setting the price for your items. ## Step 6: Receiving Sales Earnings Next, I’ll show you the process for receiving your sales earnings. Remember, to request a payout, you must have a minimum balance of $50. ### Accessing Your Sales Information On the top right corner, under your profile, click “Sales.” Select the “INFO” tab. Here, you will fill in your personal information. To enable the form, click the “Create” button. Fill in your First Name, Last Name, Country, Address, City, ZIP code, and your PayPal account. ### Tax Information Under TAX INFORMATION, select "Non-US seller (Individual)." Now, click the download link to download the WABN form. To receive payments as a creator outside the U.S., you need to complete the form. ## Filling Out the WABN Form Here is a summary of how to fill it out correctly: - **Identification**: - Field 1: Add your full name as on your document. - Field 2: Country of Citizenship (e.g., Brazil). - Field 3: Add your full address. - Field 4: Complete only if your mailing address differs from your permanent address. - Field 6A: Enter your national ID Number. - Field 6B: Check the box if you do not have an ITIN number. - **Tax Benefits**: - Part 2: Enter your country in Field 9 and leave the other fields in the section blank. - **Certification**: - Part 3: Sign your name and write the date using the month, day, and year format. Once completed, save the form to your computer. ### Submitting the Form Return to the CONNECT page. Click “Choose File,” upload the form, and click “Submit.” The form is valid for three years. After that, you’ll need to update it to keep your information current. Just keep in mind: if you submit it after the 15th of the month, your payment might be delayed until the following month. You can find a link with detailed instructions for filling out the form in the video description. ## Conclusion Now you know how to publish and sell your assets on CONNECT, along with how the fees and payment process work. If you have any questions, check the links in the description or reach out to our support team. See you next time! ```

summary: # How To Create A Custom Avatar In Avatar Editor Welcome to the CL tutorial! In this tutorial, we'll walk you through creating a customized avatar using the Avatar Editor feature. ## Loading the Default Avatar First, load the default female avatar from the CL library avatar folder. Then, click on "Avatar" in the main menu bar and select "Avatar Editor" to open the window. ## Inputting Measurements The size chart is located at the bottom of the window. We will start by inputting the width and height measurements. - **Underbust:** 28 - **Total Height:** 66 As you can see, once these values are input, the circumference, height, and length values below are automatically adjusted. This is because CL uses algorithm-based data to find the most natural body shape based on the width and height we've just entered. Next, let’s also enter the inseam value to create a more accurate body shape. ## Displaying All Measurements Now, click on the "Show All Measurements" icon. This will display all the deactivated items. ### Adjusting Height Measurements Let’s start with the items under the height category. The automatically populated bust height is already quite close to the value in the size chart. This indicates that the algorithm-based data is effectively reflecting the body shape of a real human figure. You can activate the measurement and input your value if you need more detailed adjustments. Since the difference is within the tolerance range, we will leave it as it is. #### Waist Height Adjustment Next is waist height. Here, you can see a difference compared to the size chart of about an inch or more. In this case, the size needs to be adjusted. To do so, it is recommended to first adjust the measure line to match the chart. Then activate and enter your measurement. 1. To adjust the measure line, use the "Edit Measure" tool. 2. Click on the waist measure line and drag it downward. As you do this, you'll notice that the waist height value in the Avatar Editor adjusts accordingly. Try to match it with the value in the size chart. Now, compare the measurement value with the adjusted line. If the algorithm-generated value is within the tolerance range, you can keep it. Otherwise, you can always apply the exact value from the chart. ## Adjusting Hip Measurements Just like with the waist, you can also adjust the measure lines of high hip and low hip. If there's a slight discrepancy between the chart and the current values, simply drag the lines to align them with the size chart. ## Setting Measurement Details Once you have finished adjusting the height-related items, let’s now move to set details to activate specific measurement fields. In the checkbox list, you can select the size items you wish to enter manually. One thing to note is that the center back neck-to-wrist value under length is calculated by adding the arm length and half of the across-shoulder center back neck values. Therefore, instead of entering all three values, we recommend entering either the value of center back neck to wrist or arm length and across shoulder center back neck. ## Completing the Avatar Once done, close the window. Now, complete the avatar by entering the values for the size chart in the active items. We hope that this tutorial helps you build your own avatar using your size chart. Thank you for watching!

summary: ```markdown # Garment Display Settings & Default File | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have a great update to share with you all regarding our file-saving project files and garment files. So, let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn! ## Project File Updates In our last release, we made a fantastic update where your toggle menu and display settings can now be saved within the ZFAB file, specifically the Z project file. We have also implemented this feature for garments as well. ## Demonstration of Garment Settings Let's change some settings around. For example, I will go to quality render, and I like all of these options. Next, I will hide my avatar. Even though this is a garment, it doesn't really matter. Now, I will go to **File > Save As Garment**. I can then navigate to my desktop, create a new project, and then go to **File > Open Garment** to open this up. It will automatically load with all of my garment settings right here. For instance, maybe I don’t want to show baselines or the 3D pen; I always want quality render. Additionally, I can include the avatar. Let’s say I know it's always going to be added to the workspace for the whole company. ## Saving Default Display Settings Now, I will delete this and go to **File > Save As > Project**, naming this "Default Display." After that, I will go to **Settings > User Settings > Default Files > Project File** and open the "Default Display" file. By selecting this file, it will always open every time I create a new project. I will hit close and exit out of Clo. ## Setting Up Default Views You can set this up so that every time you open Clo, you see a specific avatar and certain toggle menus. Just go to **User Settings > Default Files**, and select what you want your default project file to always be. You can reopen your assets and revert to your regular default configurations. This setup allows you to always have a particular avatar and view prepared whenever you open a new file. ## Overriding Display Settings Now, I can go to **File > Open Garment**. The garment with the display settings that I have will override because I have checked the box on display settings. I will hit okay, and now that project file's garment file display settings will be viewed. ## Conclusion So, yes, this is really cool and incredibly helpful! Thank you so much for watching. Keep having fun in Clo, and thanks so much! ```

summary: # Clo Virtual Summit: EMEA and North America 2025 ## Introduction Hi everyone, and welcome to the CLO Virtual Summit 2025. I am Laura Martinez, CX Manager for CLO Europe, and I'm happy to be kicking off this second edition with all of you. Today, we are connecting creators, students, and independent designers united by a shared passion for digital fashion and innovation. This year's theme, *From Sketch to Reality*, is all about empowering individuals to bring their ideas to life using CLO. So whether you are just starting out or already building your career in 3D fashion, this summit is designed to inspire, educate, and connect. You will hear not only from incredible speakers who will share their journeys, creative processes, and practical tips, but we will also explore tools like CLO Academy, our new community space in Connect, and initiatives like the Gloify Certificate and the Rising Talent Contest. Don't forget to check the CLO roadmap and key features, where you will discover the latest updates regarding CLO. Feel free to use the live chat throughout the session if you have any questions or thoughts; we are here and happy to engage with you. We will also be launching a few quick polls during the event, so if you want to share your opinion or help us shape future experiences, we would love to hear from you. Get ready to discover new workflows and learn how CLO can support you in shaping your future in fashion. Let's dive in! ## Speaker Introduction: Anna Cordova Hello, my name is Anna Cordova. I am a fashion and graphic designer from Spain, now based in London. My work is at the intersection of fashion and technology, and while my background is actually in fashion design, I see my work evolving into a broader exploration of responsive technologies, AI, and material science. I have been a CLO user since 2020, first as part of my practice, and now I also teach it at a university level here in London. ### Education Background I started studying fashion back in 2016 in Madrid. After two years, one of my tutors encouraged me to apply to Central St. Martins. I got in, started with a foundation year, and then went on to do the BA in Fashion Print. Between my second and third year, I had my placement year, which means I went out and worked in the industry. I spent six months at Leare in Paris, which is part of the Chanel group. In total, I spent seven years studying fashion and graduated in 2023. ### Career Development Right after graduating, I launched my own business in the UK under the name of Anacordova Studio. While working freelance for private clients and students worldwide, I knew I wanted to develop my 3D skills further. So, I enrolled in an intensive closed certificate program at Parsons, and I also got a residency at my university, which is a maker space based in Somerset House here in London, to keep building my 3D work. Later that same year, I joined the wearable technology program at Fabric Academy, where I began exploring detailed fabrication, electronics, and smart textiles, all with the goal of merging design and technology more deeply into my practice. ## The Journey to 3D Fashion ### The Impact of 3D Printing So why 3D? Everything started in 2020. I come from a large family; I have four brothers, and during the pandemic, the oldest one organized a crowdfunding campaign to buy 133 printers for our home in Madrid. Over the course of three months, we produced over 3,000 masks for local hospitals. That experience made me realize the impact of 3D printing. I was amazed by the idea of being able to design something virtually and then bring those concepts to life as tangible, functional objects. When the lockdown ended, I returned to London to continue my studies at CSM. After what I had experienced with 3D printing, CLO just felt like the natural next step. I remember asking my tutor, Alisa Palamino, if we could include CLO in the curriculum, but at that time, there wasn't much awareness of how powerful it could be for fashion design. Some still saw it as something more technical or mainly used for gaming, so I decided to teach myself using the CLO YouTube channel. ### First Project with CLO The first time I used CLO for a project was one I developed around the idea of dreams—how our brains connect random fragments while we sleep. I worked with digital mistakes from the software and started mixing familiar pattern blocks, like t-shirts or jackets, twisting them into completely new silhouettes. It was the first time I truly saw how technology could inspire design and not just support it. My interest in technology and innovation opened incredible opportunities. In my second year, I won a Chanel competition with a 3D-printed dress I designed. As part of the prize, I worked with them in Paris for six months. The concept behind the dress was to reinterpret some of the brand's most iconic elements, such as feathers or camellias, by using 3D printing to replicate their beauty without relying on animal materials. ## Notable Projects ### Collaboration with Elisa Palamino Another project that meant a lot to me was working with Elisa Palamino on a detailed recreation of a traditional Inuit fish skin robe, which was later presented during the Responsible Fashion Series at the University of Antwerp. At the time, I was still teaching myself both CLO and Blender, and my skills were basic, but Elisa invited me to collaborate on this personal project, which became a huge learning experience. I used CLO for the pattern cutting and garment simulation and Blender for designing the scene and creating the final animation. That project reminded me that digital fashion doesn't just have to be something new or about the future, but it can also be a tool to protect, educate, and remember. ### Final Collection: The Nexus Paradox My final collection at Central Saint Martins was called *The Nexus Paradox* and was presented in 2023. The Nexus Paradox aimed to explore the blurred line between humanity and technology in the digital age, translating the essence of a digital existence into a physical form. One of the key pieces of my collection was the 3D-printed dress featured on the cover of Vogue Portugal last year. The process behind this dress began in CLO, where I used the fabric simulations to experiment with shape and structure. I then exported the patterns into Blender, where I broke them into smaller printable pieces and prepared the geometry for production. Using my home 3D printer, which is pretty small, I could only print small pieces at a time—about 45 individual pieces, each taking around nine hours to print. Once printed, I assembled everything by hand using metal rings. The collection received significant interest from stylists after the CSM show, leading to collaborations. ## Teaching and Community Engagement After graduation, I submitted pieces from the Nexus Paradox to the BF competition in Spain. I started with a 3D-printed bag and developed two new looks: a corset and a replica of my final collection dress made entirely from printed pieces. I needed to replicate the dress because I had the original in London, and it was impossible to ship it to Bilbao. So, I printed all the individual pieces again, shipped them to Bilbao, and assembled everything once I was there. Today, I teach CLO at universities like Central Saint Martins, the University of the Arts London, and Instituto Marangoni. I also run my short course at Central Saint Martins called *Creative CLO 3D for Absolute Beginners*, where I welcome individuals from all kinds of backgrounds who are simply interested in digital fashion. Teaching keeps me constantly learning, as I need to stay up-to-date with any new updates. ### Student Work and Industry Demand Many of my students start with ambitious sketches, and CLO helps them understand what is possible—what fits, what moves, and what doesn’t. Whether someone wants to work in gaming, performance wear, or sustainable production, I feel CLO is becoming an essential part of how we design today. Many of my students build their ideas digitally in CLO, experimenting with silhouette, proportion, or even fabrics before bringing them into the real world. Some even print their patterns from CLO and create physical replicas of their virtual designs. This process, known as digital designing, ends up with both a physical garment and a virtual replica of it. It's exciting to see how students don’t use CLO just as a visualization tool but as an integral part of the creative and technical development. ## Conclusion Right now, I feel 3D fashion skills are in high demand. More and more brands are integrating virtual design into their workflows, whether for sustainability, speed, or marketing. However, even though the industry is shifting, there is still a significant gap in skilled professionals. I believe it's a great moment for young designers to step in, and the truth is that you don’t need to be an expert to get started. My advice is to begin with small projects, follow tutorials online, and allow yourself to experiment. Don’t aim for a perfect render at first; focus on understanding how everything works. Connecting with others online can also be beneficial. Sharing your work and collaborating has been a huge part of my growth, and it’s where most of my work opportunities have come from. I don’t see CLO or digital fashion as just tools; for me, they are ways to ask better questions—to rethink how we design, who we design for, and how our work shows up in the world. It’s not about replacing the physical; I believe technology adds to what is real and helps us imagine new possibilities. Thank you for your time today, and I look forward to connecting with you! ## CLO Academy Overview To get started with

summary: ```markdown # 3D Topstitch Schematic Render | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have some great updates to share with you on our schematic render. So, let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn. ## Accessing Schematic Render Here I have this wonderful garment. It's all set up. No, it is not in schematic render, but we're about to enter schematic render. To get to schematic render, I'm going to go to my 3D toggle menu over here. I'm going to select the second option at the top. And now it's in schematic. ## Updates in Schematic Render Look at that schematic! We've made some updates with our top stitching. If I go to my schematic window, you can always increase your silhouette line and pixels there. You can increase your seam line thickness as well. Additionally, you can increase your internal line or decrease it. You can hide it if you want to hide it or show it. Also, you can increase your top stitching. ### Top Stitching Options We've also added in more options for increasing top stitching if you'd like. Before I get into more of the top stitching, just know you can right here. If you have any questions with top stitching, there's a little eye icon. Hover over that, and it will give you all of this information that you can customize more of your modifications in your property editor. As a reminder, you can change your line color here. You can also decide if you want your garment texture or color, and you can play around with your brightness. For a sketch look, you might want to have that brightness high and choose a white color. ## Control in Schematic It's important to note about schematic, as I think a lot of people forget about this or don’t really know. Jumping into my 2D window, you have a lot of control when it comes to schematic. If you go to your edit pattern piece, you can select different lines. I'm holding down Shift and selecting them. In your property editor, you can then decide to show your schematic line or not. If I uncheck this because I don't want to show it, then it won't be seen over here. Conversely, if I select this line here and go down into my property editor, I can check the "Show schematic line" option, and now I'll see it. ### Customizing Line Visibility You have complete control over which lines you want to see. Just select the line using your edit pattern tool and then show or hide any of these lines. You even have control over the Z offset and how far out you want it to be. For example, I increased the Z offset a lot on this shoulder, and now this line is really far out. I can also decrease this to zero, and that will be fine too. You have a lot of control over this. Sometimes you want certain internal lines visible; sometimes you won’t. For this one, I might want this internal line, so I’ll turn on schematic render for that, but for others, I might decide I don’t want that. ## Managing Top Stitches Now, what I can do that's new is control over my top stitches. To access control over your top stitches, go to the top stitch option at the very top in your object browser. I will select all of them right now by holding down Shift. In my property editor, under "Local Schematic Scale," I can turn this on or off. If I turn this off, then you're going to see my top stitches change a lot, becoming really tiny. I can turn this back on again. ### Adjusting Top Stitch Properties Now, I have control over various parts of the top stitches, including length, spacing, offset, thickness, width, and distance. I will change all these back to 100 just so you can see how we can adjust and play around with this. **Length**: This is the length of the stitch itself. For instance, if I want the length of the stitch to be much longer for better visibility, I can set it to 200 and hit enter. **Spacing**: To avoid a straight line appearance, I can increase the spacing, say to 150, which improves visibility when I zoom out. **Offset**: This is how far away it is from the line. Setting this to 120, or even 170 for a more noticeable effect, allows for better visual distinction. **Thickness**: I might want the thickness to be 170 for better visibility. **Width Percentage**: If I set this to 200, it appears much thicker, but I prefer 115 for a more balanced look. **Distance Percentage**: Adjusting this will determine how much distance you want between stitches. A larger value can show a significant difference, but I generally prefer to keep it at 100. ### Customized Adjustments Now, I can easily see the type of stitching I want. For single top stitches, I can adjust the offset to be 115 or even 150 for better visibility. I can also increase the spacing to 190 for distinction. Similarly, for double needle top stitches, I might want to set the offset to 125. The flexibility to adjust specific top stitches or all of them together is quite beneficial. ## Important Notes One crucial thing to note is that the moment I hide schematic, the adjustments made apply only to the schematic top stitch visual and do not affect the actual top stitch. The underlying details on how the top stitch should be constructed are retained within the top stitch itself. All the adjustments made are solely for the visual effect in the schematic. So, the local schematic scale is distinct from the actual top stitch information, which remains unchanged and will be included in your tech pack. ## Conclusion Thanks so much for watching! If you have any questions, use that comment section down below. Don't forget to like and subscribe, and keep having fun with Clo! ```

summary: # Clo User Story – Calida ## Introduction Kita, for me, is high quality, super comfy, and well-fitting underwear, nightwear, and loungewear. ## Team Overview I’m Favin Moi and I'm leading the technical product development team at Calida. This team includes our pattern makers and 3D developers. ## Implementation of 3D Workflows In the beginning of 2021, we set up workarounds and workflows into our company using 3D technology across different departments. This includes: - Hollow constructions - Packaging - Vision merchandising guidelines ### Challenges Before Clo Before we implemented Clo, I always had to wait for the sewing samples to see if my pattern was good and if I had placed the right lines correctly. ## Benefits of Using Clo Now, I can create the pattern, bring it into Clo, and check the avatar to see if everything is correct and in the right place. This has allowed us to save on samples and time, which is a significant advantage. ### Enhanced Collaboration The integration of Clo 3D has resulted in closer, or even new, collaborations between various departments, such as: - Technical product development with the design team - Visual merchandising, which we didn't have before ## Development of Kids Collection Another benefit of using Clo is that, for developing the kids' collection, I can easily place the motive prints and check the size and placement. This clarity is beneficial for everyone involved in the design process, including the sales team. ### Efficiency in Visual Merchandising We have also seen significant improvements in visual merchandising since implementing Clo. We are now faster than before because combinations or changes can be made rapidly in 3D. This efficiency allows us to save money and reduce the effort required to order items that we might not ultimately use for display. ## Future Plans We are continuing to build up our libraries and perfect them, with the goal of having our entire collection in 3D. I genuinely believe that 3D technology is and will be the future of garment manufacturing. ## Conclusion We are really happy with the progress and grateful to Clo for their excellent support.

summary: ```markdown # Set Grade Point | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have some great new updates to share with you about grading. So, let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn! ## New Grading Updates First, let's talk about some new fun updates we have with grading. Right now, I have monochrome here, but if I switch to the front texture surface, I'll see that I have a graphic. If I go over to my toggle menu, which I use to switch out of monochrome surface to texture, I can then go to this t-shirt here and say "Show Grading." Now, I can see all of my grading and even my graphics, too. This feature allows you to see all of your grading at once, which is really nice and helpful. ### Accessing Grading To access this feature, go to your toggle in your 2D window, select your garment display (the little t-shirt), and then choose "Show Grading." This way, you can see grading even if you aren't selecting a grading tool. ## Defining Grading Points Now, I'm going to talk about some more in-depth aspects of grading, especially the define grading point feature that we just added in version 2025.1. ### Edit Grading Tools I'm going to go to my edit grading tools and select "Edit Grading." Once I select this, I'll see all the grading immediately, and all of my points will have a green halo around them. This indicates that these points are graded points. Everything that is green has a graded point. Initially, this caused some frustration because if I selected a point and then increased or decreased it, you could see how just that one part is changing. You might be thinking, "Why is this happening?" Don't worry, we fixed it! ## Understanding Internal Lines What you might be seeing are internal lines. You just have to make sure you grade your internal lines. There are actually quite a lot of curve points here. You might ask, "How do you know that?" Well, I helped develop the software, so that's how I know some of these things! However, you can also find out by going to "Edit Curve Grading," where you'll see the graded red dots with the green halo. ### Selecting Multiple Points If you hold down Shift, you can select all of these points at once. This old method allows you to select multiple points, which can be more efficient. ## Converting Points Now, you might be thinking, "I don't want to go through that long process." Instead, you can select the red dots. Hold down Shift while left-clicking on each red dot. After selecting, release Shift, and then right-click on one of these points. A dropdown menu will appear, and you can select "Convert to Non-Graded Point." ### Checking Your Work Now, on the left side, all of these curve points are still graded, but on the right side, they are not. When you click on a point and increase it, everything is graded proportionally. If you mistakenly miss a point, don't worry—everybody makes mistakes! Just go back to your edit grading, select your missed point, and increase it. You can also use Ctrl + Z to undo. ## Best Practices for Grading ### Selecting Curve Points To make the grading process efficient, go into your edit curve point tool and check how many curve points you've got. If there are too many, with your edit pattern tool, select the whole neck opening, right-click on top of the line, and choose "Optimize Curve Points." This will help streamline your workflow. ### Proportional Grading After optimizing, you can move your points, and they will grade proportionally together. You can use your arrow keys to adjust the grading increments for precise control. ## Importing DXF Patterns Let's say you want to import a DXF pattern. I'm going to show you a nice workflow for this. After importing, check your curve points. If there are still many curve points, you can go to your edit pattern tool, select the front and back, and right-click to optimize them. ### Grading After Import Once optimized, you can go into your grading tools. If the green halo isn't around the curve points, it means they aren't graded, which is great for fast grading without concerns about proportionality. ## Conclusion Thank you so much for watching! If you have any questions, use the comment section down below. Don't forget to like and subscribe. There are so many great videos to help you out on your clothing journey. Keep having fun in Clo! Thanks again! ```
