summary: # Clo Ai Studio | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe, and I'm going to talk all about our AI features, how to access them, how to use them, and everything AI. So, let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn. ## Accessing the AI Features Okay, so I have my screen in front of me here. If you don't have anything activated or on, this is probably what you're going to see. You'll likely see some grayed-out versions of our old AI logo and everything there. So, it's going to be grayed out. If you click on it or anything, nothing will happen. If you hover over it, you'll get some information indicating that this AI plugin is not activated. To activate it, you have to go to your CL admin. You'll see this for any of the AI features. For instance, if I select my fabric here, the magic wand is deactivated. Again, if you hover over it, there will be some guidance for you. If I go into my render window, you'll see that it is grayed out here as well. So anywhere that the magic wand for AI is located, it's currently grayed out. Now you might be wondering, “How do I get there?” I’m going to show you how to access it if you're an enterprise user or an individual user. ## Enterprise User Access Let's first start with the Enterprise. I’m going to open up and go to Chlo. Here, I'm in Chlooop, and you have to go to your page. If you're not an admin, you need to ask your admin to grant access. But if you are an admin, listen up. You'll go to your profile and log in. Once logged in, go to your account page. As an admin, I can access my license account admin. So, I’m going to retype in my password and then go to my AI Studio plugin. Once I select this, I’ll see everything is inactive. If I want to change that, I’ll go to edit and choose what I want on or off. I want all of my AI, so I’m going to turn all of this on and hit save. It will show a successful update. You might get a popup asking you to confirm your understanding that using this externally is on you, not on Chlo. Once that’s set, you’ll hit okay. Now, as you know, this is my enterprise login, and I don’t see this. That's because I have to exit and minimize because this is my individual account. Then I’ll have to open it up again. ## Individual User Access For individuals, you have your Clo, and you're probably seeing grayed-out AI options. You can hover over and go to Clo admin. This will direct you to your admin page. Once there, go straight to the AI Studio plugin and hit edit. You might get a popup saying you need to confirm your acceptance of the terms. After that, you can select whichever options you want active or inactive. Hit save, hit okay, and again, exit and reopen Clo. As you can see, here’s my enterprise, and I now have access to all of my AI. The same process applies to individual users. Just need to reopen your Clo, and you'll have access to the AI features you activated. ## Overview of AI Features Now, let's dive into the different AI features we have. We’ll start with AI Studio, which is currently in beta. Here, I can see all my options and features, including what's new in embroidery. ### AI Graphics Generator Let’s start with the AI graphics generator. How does it work? It’s set up similarly to all of our AI features. You can select either image or text. I’m going to stick with text. I want to create a pop art design, so I’ll type in "lion face" and hit generate. Look at that! I can generate multiple versions and pin the one I want to keep. Alternatively, I can hit random prompt for a completely new idea. Just remember, the content will change if you do that. Once I find a design I like, I can apply it to my graphics. I can also check my history of generated graphics by clicking on the clock icon. ### Embroidery Feature I can upload an image and convert it to embroidery. For instance, if I upload a pineapple image and hit preview, I’ll see the embroidery version. If I want to try another design, I can upload a different image and preview that as well. ### Texture Creation Next, let’s check out texture options. I can select my fabric type, say a canvas, and choose a pattern. For example, I’ll select "tartan check" with a pattern size of one and generate it. To visualize better, I can add a project file and apply my chosen pattern to the fabric. The pattern size is critical; it influences the dimensions of the design. For instance, if you choose size one, the pattern is close to 1024 pixels. If you choose size four, it scales up accordingly. ### Pattern Drafter Now let’s jump to the 2D pattern drafter. I can create a shirt using my measurements or upload an image to generate a pattern. For example, I can upload a sketch from a store, and the AI will generate a pattern based on that image. After uploading, I can edit the pattern as needed. The simple mode is great for those unfamiliar with measurements, linking them automatically. If you know what you’re doing, you can switch to general mode for precise editing. ### Render Feature Finally, let’s explore the render feature. I can upload a target image or use a random prompt. I’ll select one and generate it. Once generated, I can refine elements such as hair or garment details. It’s best to start with the face and then move to the background. After saving my work, I can continue adjusting or changing backgrounds as needed, ensuring my design is just right. ## Conclusion You can save all your creations and access them later, whether in the pattern drafter or render feature. Thank you so much for watching! If you have any questions, use the comment section below. Don’t forget to like and subscribe for more great videos about Clo and everything it offers. Keep having fun in CL!

summary: ```markdown # Denim Wet Wash Effect | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have a great update for all of you that involves denim. Now, this was in our 2025.1 release, and it's really cool. It provides presets for different denim washes. So, let's dive in and have some fun while we learn! ## Accessing Denim Options Okay, so here I have my Clo window open. It's looking great. What I'm going to start to do is go straight into that denim. Before I do, let's just figure out where we can find this. Over in my object browser, where the fabric is, I'm going to go to my denim fabric right here and select that. In my property editor, you'll see the fabric type option, and I'm going to select this new option: denim. Similar to our fabric option, new things are going to pop up in our property editor. So, I'm going to select denim here. Now, what you're going to see in the property editor is "wet process." The default will be "unwashed." So here, I'll see "unwashed." Now, let's go through what all of these different wash options are. ## Wash Options ### Unwashed Unwashed denim is basically like raw denim. It means there haven't been any washes or chemical applications applied to this denim. It's normally really stiff, and there isn't a lot of wear and tear. You'll see what the denim is at its most natural form. It's important to ensure that when you're looking at the denim and picking your denim, you have nice highs and lows in your texture. This is particularly crucial for unwashed denim, as having depth from the highs and lows of the weave is essential. ### Rinse Wash Next, we have a rinse wash. This will give the denim a clean and slightly softened look. It retains the original color but softens it a bit. As you can see here, my original color was dark indigo, and it just lightened it up, giving it a more worn feeling. ### Enzyme Wash An enzyme wash will slightly add more fading to it and give a more worn feeling, as you can see here. ### Stone Wash The stone wash will have a much more pronounced contrast between the highs and lows, making it more defined. This process involves putting pumice stones into your washer, which provides a lot more of a worn feeling. ### Acid Wash An acid wash creates more of a marbled effect on your denim. It involves a chemical process that gives dark splotches, resulting in a bold look. ### Bleach Wash The bleach wash will lighten the entire fabric because bleach is added. It creates near-white areas and a stark contrast between dark and light. ### Ozone Wash The ozone wash will evenly lighten everything throughout the fabric, resulting in a uniform lightening effect. This is quite different from what we just saw with the bleach wash. ### Custom Wash After the ozone wash, we have the option called custom. The custom wash allows you to bring in any map you want and start to adjust it as you like. ## Important Notes Before we move further, it's essential to know that all the effects you're seeing are visual effects. None of this is affecting the physics of the fabric at all. Down the road, we hope to have that feature, but right now, this is all visual. These are all textures laying on top of each other to create this look. This may affect the speed when you're changing different textures or adjusting them. So, please be aware that this does not physically adjust the fabric. If you want the fabric to be physically adjusted, you need to go into the physics of the fabric and adjust it yourself. This gives you that great look that many of you have been asking for us to provide and adjust. ## Adjusting Denim Wash Options Now, let's return to the fabric and look at the stone wash example. Here, I'm going to show you the different slider options you have when adjusting your denim. In my stone wash, there's one slider that will constantly change for you, which is the slider right above the blend option. This is the "fading intensity." It will change based on the type of wash you're choosing. Different washes will have different options for how you want this applied. The fading intensity directly affects your wash map and how visible that map is. The other options—absorbency, cycle duration, and seam abrasion—will affect your base color map and also the wash map. ### Cycle Duration Cycle duration is essentially how long you're saying this is going to be in the wash. The lower the duration, the darker the overall fabric will be, while a higher duration will lighten it. ### Fading Intensity The fading intensity map adjusts how intense you want the wash map to be. Increasing this means you're increasing how intense the wash effect will be, creating more contrast. ## Bleach Wash Adjustments Let's talk about the bleach wash now. Here, we're going to focus on absorbency, which determines how much of that wash solution is soaked into your fabric. The more it soaks in, the deeper it goes and the fuzzier it will appear at the edges. A good range for absorbency is between 1 and 10 for a realistic look. You can adjust it higher or lower as desired. ## Seam Abrasion Next, we have seam abrasion. Increasing this will enhance the intensity of any existing puckering on your seams. However, it won't affect the puckering itself; it simply amplifies what's already there. ## Transforming Maps With the map, I can change its size using the drop-down menu. I can adjust the aspect ratio and modify the height and width as needed. It's important to keep in mind that if you use the edit texture tool, it will change both the base map and the texture map simultaneously. ## Blending Options You can also explore different blending options. Currently, I'm using "overlay," but you can try options like "soft light," "color dodge," etc. Each blending option will give you different visual results. ## Acid Wash Color Overlay Now, let’s jump into the acid wash. If I want to change the color, I can adjust the acid concentration and select a color from my palette. When changing the whole denim color, remember to adjust the puckering colors as well for realism. ## Custom Wash Creation Now, let's go to the custom wash. I can add in a completely different wash and make adjustments. For example, I can bring in a star wash and tweak the settings like seam abrasion, cycle duration, and absorbency to achieve the desired look. ## Saving Custom Washes I can save this as a custom denim wash, which will be stored in my library for future use. ## Exploring Multiple Colorways Let's explore how different washes can work with multiple colorways. In production, I can open the colorway window and create different colorways, each using various washes. ## Using Denim Features on Other Fabrics Lastly, I want to clarify that while the features are primarily for denim, you can experiment with them on other fabric types. For instance, if I apply denim effects to a knit fabric, I can still achieve interesting results, but remember this isn't the intended use. ## Conclusion Thank you so much for watching! If you have any questions, feel free to use the comment section below. Don't forget to like and subscribe. There are so many great videos for you to learn all about how CLO works and the excellent features we offer. Thanks again, and keep having fun in CLO! ```

My name is Buun Kim, your customer experience manager. ### The Vibrant Asian Community When we look at our global community, one region consistently stands out: Asia. From the established community in Hong Kong to the rapidly growing users in Indonesia, Vietnam, and across Southeast Asia, your passion is undeniable. We see it in your incredible engagement across all our channels, from YouTube and social media to our online community and workshops. This energy is what inspires us to be closer to you. In recognition of this, we opened our Jakarta office last year and this year proudly expanded with a new office in Ho Chi Minh City. ### Summit Purpose And that brings us to today. This summit is our way of saying that your creativity and impact deserve a stage. It is our promise to empower you, the very creators who are shaping what comes next, and to provide a dedicated space for this incredible community to connect, share, and thrive. Today, you'll hear inspiring stories and practical tips from experts in your region, all designed to help you on your creative journey. Thank you for being such a vital part of our global story. Welcome to the summit. --- ## Major Updates in CLO Hi everyone and welcome. I'm Sunonny, a software product manager here at CLO Virtual Fashion. It's fantastic to see so many of you here today. ### Recent Updates This year has been huge for us. We've launched two major updates: CLO 2025.0 and 2025.1, packed with powerful new tools that will make creating digital garments faster and more intuitive than ever. Over the next 10 minutes, I'm going to walk you through some of the most exciting new features and show you how they can help you bring your creative visions to life, even if you're just starting out. ### CLO's Role in Digital Fashion Before we dive into the new features, let me give you a quick overview of where CLO fits in the world of digital fashion. Our ultimate goal is to empower the creation of every garment on Earth. CLO is the heart of a larger ecosystem that includes tools for everything from 3D design to creating assets for films, games, and the metaverse. We also have platforms like CLOSET, which helps you collaborate with others and bring your designs to the market. While the ecosystem is vast, our focus today is on you and how the CLO software can help you design garments quickly and easily. ### Core Principles Everything we do at CLO is guided by one simple principle: helping you design garments quickly and easily. This is the driving force behind every update and the new features. To achieve this, we focus on four key areas: 1. **Effortless and Intuitive**: Make the software feel natural and easy to use. 2. **Seamless Workflow**: Ensuring a smooth creative process from start to finish. 3. **All-in-One**: Bringing more essential tools directly into CLO. 4. **Boost Assets**: Helping you create stunning, realistic, and detailed assets. --- ## New Features Overview ### Improved User Interface Let's look at some examples of how our latest updates deliver on this promise. We believe that a great design tool should feel like an extension of your own creativity without any interruptions. That's why we focus on creating a more seamless and intuitive workspace. First, you'll notice our continuously updated interface, which is cleaner and more user-friendly. A major step in our latest 2025.1 update is the new embedded web view that's neat and has appealing visuals. This seamless experience extends to our library window, allowing you to enjoy features from CLOSET without ever having to leave the software. No more switching between windows or breaking your creative flow—everything is integrated into your workspace, saving you time and keeping you focused. ### Auto-Fitting Tool Enhancements Now for the fun part: creating garments. We've introduced some incredible new features that give you more creative freedom, regardless of your experience level. Let's start with this common task: fitting your garment onto different avatars. We've made a huge improvement to our auto-fitting tool. Now, when you resize a garment for a new avatar, CLO cleverly maintains its topology, ensuring that the mesh details remain consistent. ### Realistic Soft Body Simulation But our simulation improvements go beyond just garments. You can now apply a realistic soft body simulation to any object you import into CLO. This is a huge creative boost. Thinking about designing a realistic squishy cushion for a virtual sofa or a plush toy? This feature allows you to bring entire environments to life with incredible realism right inside CLO. ### AI-Powered Pattern Drafter What if you're new to pattern making? Our new AI-powered pattern drafter is a game changer. It allows you to create a draft of your pattern with incredible ease, helping you visualize and iterate on your ideas faster than ever before. For those who want to be more experimental, you can use the 3D pen tool to sketch garments with volume directly into the 3D window. It's an intuitive way to sculpt your designs and add a touch of artistic freedom to your work. ### Seamless Blocking Tool We're always looking to bring more functionality into CLO so you can do everything in one place. A perfect example is our seamless blocking tool. This feature lets you create seamless blocks directly within your design. While you could do this with some workarounds, it's now much faster and easier. This is especially useful for creating professional-looking knitwear. ### Enhanced Mesh Retouching We've also enhanced our mesh retouching capabilities. You now have more intuitive brush selections and a double-sided retouching option. This gives you finer control to perfect the shape and fit of your garment directly on the 3D model, ensuring that it looks exactly right from every angle. ### Customizable Export Presets When it's time to share your work, our new customizable export presets make it incredibly easy. You can now save your preferred settings for different 3D file formats, streamlining your workflow when exporting to other platforms or collaborating with others. --- ## Boosting Your Creative Assets The details are what make a design truly stand out, and we've added some amazing tools to help boost your assets. A new creative leap is here: the AI graphic generator now supports embroidery, transforming any image into realistic stitch designs you can directly use in CLO. This is just the beginning of the changes that will unlock even more customization possibilities. We've also introduced new denim wash presets. With just a few clicks, you can apply authentic washes and textures to your denim designs, saving you tons of time. Finally, we've improved zipper management so you can easily manage zipper assets within the object browser. Adjusting everything from the teeth style to the puller details is now much more precise and all handled in one convenient tab. It's these little things that make a big difference. Thank you so much for your time today. As you can see, our latest updates, 2025.0 and 2025.1, are all about empowering you to design garments quickly and easily. I encourage you to jump in and explore these new features for yourself. For more detailed tutorials and inspiration, be sure to visit the CLO website and subscribe to our YouTube channel. The world of digital fashion is constantly evolving, and we're committed to providing you with the latest tools to be a part of it. We can't wait to see the incredible designs you create. Thank you! --- ## Animation Techniques in CLO Hi everyone! I'm thrilled to have you here at our virtual summit. I'm Tracy Ho, and together with my colleague Chester, today we are going to explore how to take your animations from concepts to creation using CLO. Whether you are a beginner or looking to refine your skills, I've got valuable insights to help you bring your ideas to life. ### Key Elements of Animation To begin, let's discuss the five key elements that will guide us through this journey: preparations, motions, environment, lighting, and output. Mastering these elements will help you transform your concepts into captivating animations. #### Preparations Preparations are essential steps in our creative process. We want to ensure our garments are styled and stable, and for that, we can use the tag function by tacking a transparent fabric onto your avatar. You can attach and secure trims as accessories so they stay in place during movement. It is also important to tack accessories onto the garments of your avatars to keep everything intact. Tacking parts together helps prevent distortion during animation, making the fabric look natural. Plus, you can tag garments to your avatar's hands to create interactions between your characters and the clothing. Using the tack function gives your animations a solid foundation, ensuring your design stays in place throughout the process. #### Adding Motion Now that we have prepared our garment, it's time to add some motion. Motion is what makes our animation lively and exciting. In addition to using the built-in motions in CLO, you can also download FBX motion data from Mixamo or other platforms. This gives you a range of natural movements to use in your animations. You can also use wind controllers to make garments flutter as if they're in a breeze, which adds realism to your scene. Another useful technique is OBJ Mate, which lets you switch poses smoothly for better transitions between different shapes. Using these motion techniques will turn your static designs into captivating animations. #### Crafting the Environment Next, let's focus on the environment. summary: ```markdown # Soft Body Simulation Improvement | Clo 2025.1 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I have some great updates to share with you on our soft body simulation features. I'm just going to hide my patterns. This avatar is not rigged at all. I can go over here to my toggle menu and select my avatar, then choose "Show Avatar Joints," and you'll see that there really aren't any joints present. ### Turning on Soft Body Simulation Now, I can select this avatar or OBJ and go into my property editor over here to turn on soft body simulation. Now that I have this on, I can play around with this slider to adjust the stiffness. I can make it really plushy or increase it so it's really stiff. The higher I go, the stiffer it is; the lower I go, the less stiff it is. I'm going to set it pretty low. ### Simulating the Soft Body Now, I'm just going to hit simulate, and you'll see in real-time how this starts to bounce, conform a bit, and get squishy. I'll show my garment pattern pieces. To do that, I'm just going to hit Shift + W. That's the shortcut. I could also go into my toggle over in garment display and say "Show Garment." ### Interacting with the Simulation What I can do here is click on my pattern pieces, and you'll see how they start to move in. As you can see, my avatar also starts to get deformed and pushed in. If I hide this, do you see how it's moving around? It's really cool what this can do. Now, what's also nice is if I select this avatar and change the stiffness up, you'll see in real-time how it's changing. ## Practical Applications So now we kind of understand how it works. Let's jump into how you could practically use it. Here, I have my garment, and I'm going to bring in some shoulder pads. I'm also thinking this could be great for bras and backpacks. I'm going to show you the shoulder pad example because I created that OBJ, and it works well. ### Importing the OBJ I'm going to go to File, then Import OBJ. One thing to know is if you're going to import your OBJ, just make sure that it is a clean OBJ. There should be no intersections and no holes. If you do have holes or intersections, then the soft body simulation won't be possible. ### Adjusting the Shoulder Pads Here, I'm just going to select this and first make these a little bit smaller because they are a bit too big. Then I'm going to move them over and start to place them where I want them to be. Nice! Before I turn on any soft body simulation, I'm just going to simulate and let my garment sit on this new OBJ to get everything set up. ### Simulating the Shoulder Pads Cool! Then I can simulate again. ## Handling Mesh Issues Before we finish up, I just want to show you really quickly what will happen if I try to bring in an OBJ that has some issues with its mesh. If I go to import and select an OBJ that has problems, if I turn on soft body and hit simulate, a warning is going to come up, telling me there are open hole issues and self-intersections. ### Visualizing Mesh Issues I can hit okay, and by going into my toggle menu again, I’ll hit "Show Wireframe." summary: ```markdown # Save Display Settings | Clo 2025.0 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and I'm going to go through one of these really cool updates we have with our UI and saving out the toggle menu and how all of that works. So, let's jump on in and have some fun while we learn. ## Overview of the Toggle Menu Here I have a complete blank screen. Just so you guys all know, we're going to first break down how this works for you. Then I'm going to tell you some things you need to know about it and also walk you through how it could help in a workflow. ## How It Works It works pretty easily. If I just drag and drop this file in here, automatically, it's going to open up with my project files toggle menu, just like how I saved it. So, when I drop it into an empty workspace, Flow is just going to bring in how you saved your project file. That is the default for just bringing it into a new club. ### Handling Existing Files Now, if I have something in here already and I drag and drop a project file in like this, a popup's going to come up. This is when you get to decide. Right down here, there's something called display settings. That's what the toggle menus are. If I check this on the display settings that I saved with the project file, however I saved it with the display settings checked on and off is what will then show up. If I have this checked on and I hit okay, those project file display settings will then appear. As you can see, the toggle menu is a bit different. Now, if I go back to this one and drop it in and uncheck this, the default display settings will be used. Just wanted to repeat that: the default display settings will be used. ## Default Display Settings This is the default display settings. As you can see, it was very different from the first time we saw this file. The first time we saw this file looked completely different. Now, when we see this file, it looks like this because these are the defaults. ### Default Settings Breakdown - **Quality Render:** Off - **Schematic Render:** Off - **Garment Display:** Almost everything checked on except "Show 2D Measurements" and "Show Garment Fitting Suit." - **Trim Display:** Everything on. - **Avatar:** "Show Avatar" and "Show 3D Pen Avatar." - **Fabric:** Textured surface (not thick textured surface). - **Fit Maps:** Off. - **Avatar Surface:** Textured surface. - **Environment:** "Show 3D Ground Shadow" and "Show Ground Grid." ## Practical Applications You're probably asking me, "All right, Phoebe, why is this helpful for setting quality standards or anything like that?" Think about it this way. Here I have my garment, and next time I open it, I want to kind of do sketching or pass it to someone who wants to view it as a sketch. Maybe they're going into a fitting and want to see the fit maps. That's when I would turn on schematic and the first stressor strain map. I might also say, "I don't want to see the avatar because I want to focus on the garment." I would also hide the turn lines and baselines, and I don't want to see pins. However, I would say, "Show 2D measurements if you have them." ### Saving Project Settings Once I've set this up, I can hit File, Save As Project, and save it as "Fitting." This will then be saved, and the tech designer or fit person will have it all ready and prepared for them. You could also do this if brands and vendors are working together. Maybe you tell vendors that in Stage One, you have to show all pins and all strength. In the final stage, you want to ensure that "Quality Render" is turned on, "Schematics" turned off, and the avatar is always hidden when you send it out. This way, you'll always see the project file how you want it seen in that stage. ## Important Notes Just know one thing: this only works for project files. If you're using an old file made before 2025, you have to save it first, and then the toggle will be saved to that project file. If you bring in a 2024.1 version, you won't have this option, and the default settings will automatically show up. ## Conclusion That is just some fun facts to know. Thank you so much for watching. I hope this helped. If you have any questions, use that comment section below. Don't forget to like and subscribe! There are so many great videos for you to watch about all of these great features and everything. Thanks again for watching, and I hope you had fun! ```

summary: # How To Activate AI Studio In CLO 2025.1 ## Introduction Hi everyone, my name is Ariel, and today I'm going to be talking about how to activate or turn on the new AI Studio in CLO 2025.1. ## Overview of AI Features If you have updated to 2025.1, you may have noticed that many of the AI features and buttons have been grayed out, or all of the AI features have been moved into the AI Studio located in the upper right-hand corner. This pink button is situated next to the new location of the CLO library. ## Logging Into Your CLO Account In order to activate this button, which will enable all the studio features, you first need to log in to your CLO account at [clo3d.com](https://www.clo3d.com). ### Step-by-Step Login 1. Navigate to [clo3d.com](https://www.clo3d.com). 2. Log in as you normally would through the Closet link. ## Accessing the AI Studio Plugin Once you're logged in, head to the upper right-hand corner, which will take you to your account page. ### Locating the AI Studio Plugin On your account page, look at the left-hand side. As you scroll down with your cursor, you will notice a new option called the **AI Studio plugin**. summary: # Clo 2025.1 Features Highlights ## Introduction Hey everyone, it's Phoebe here, and we have some amazing new features in Clo that will help you be more productive and creative at the same time. So, let's jump on in and have some fun while we learn all about this new 2025.1 release. ## 3D Pen Tool Enhancements Drawing on the avatar using our 3D pen tool allows you to create ideas within Clo even without pattern knowledge. With this update, we have expanded the tool to allow you to create garments that have volume within them. Instead of only drawing directly on the avatar, simply use the shortcut **P** and start drawing off the avatar. All of the other great shortcuts will still be available to you, along with some new ones, like adding a circle around the avatar or showing the distance from your point to the avatar. Before you know it, you will have drawn a garment within Clo, using the flattening tool to translate these lines into patterns. Clo will then sew and arrange the patterns for you. Start adding fabrics, and just like that, you have a garment. ## Denim Wash Presets The tedious work of creating washes is over. Now, within Clo, there are eight different denim wash presets for you to adjust and test out. The options include: - Unwashed - Rinse - Enzyme - Stone - Acid - Bleach - Ozone - Custom Each wash will have different slider options to adjust based on the selected wash, including a cycle time option and a seam abrasion option. If you want to use your own maps for a wash, the custom option is for you. Here, you can add in your own map and use the sliders to adjust the wash accordingly. When adjusting the cycle time option, remember that the longer the time, the lighter the wash will become. For all the wash options, you will also be able to change the colors as well. Create custom, visually realistic-looking denim within minutes that will impress everyone. ## Texture and Seamless Garment Creation Ever wanted to test out different textures and colors within the pattern without going through the work of cutting and sewing the pattern pieces? Now you can! This feature was specifically designed to help all our knitwear designers get closer to designing and creating seamless garments within Clo, with a multitude of different workflows to create these new seamless blocking lines. The options are endless for creating seamless garments. The tracing tool will trace out internal baselines to seamless lines. The edit pattern tool will allow you to offset as a seamless line. Finally, the seamless line tool itself will allow you to create seamless lines on your patterns. Going into the object browser, you can either assign the fabric or drag and drop it onto the pattern. You will also have the ability to adjust the lines you created using the edit or transform pattern tools. You can also adjust the texture within each seamless block panel through the edit texture tool, both individually or collectively. By the end, I can create a much more interesting garment quickly and easily, all without cutting a single pattern. Now that's what I call seamless! ## Soft Body Physics Now you can apply soft body to non-skeleton OBJs, opening up a whole new world of options like pillows or foam. You can see here that when turning on the soft body, the shape of the avatar actually adjusts and changes due to the fabric. This improvement could also be applied to trims like shoulder pads. Bringing these in as an OBJ, I can apply the soft body effect to them, and now a foam-like effect is applied. Using the slider, I can control the softness amount, improving the realism of the garments created within Clo. ## Schematic Render Options We have updated our schematic render option for top stitches to make a more sketch-like feel to help support tech packs better. Within the top stitch property editor, you can turn on the option for schematic scale and start to edit different visual options like length, spacing, offset, thickness, width, and distance, making the top stitches much easier to view and see within the schematic render. ## Library and Asset Management In Clo, we have updated our library further. The new library is still in the upper right-hand corner, but now when you open it, you will see an entire new tab just for Connect. Within this tab, you will be able to view all your purchases along with all of the great assets that are within the website. Using the filter option, you can filter through all of the available assets within Connect and narrow down what you are specifically looking for. We have also improved our layout of Clo within the new library to mimic our closet layout, making it easier to navigate and find your projects. All our generative AI features can now be found within the AI button next to the library for easier access to our AI suite. The process and steps to use these AI features have not changed. ## AI Render Enhancements Here, I will use the AI render enhancer as an example. Just as before, I can upload a rendered image into my workspace. Using the prompts section, I can cycle through different AI faces by either writing in or autogenerating random prompts. Once a face is chosen, you can preview this and even continue to refine the image using our updated refinement options to get an even more realistic-looking face. The new background option from our last release can also be found here. I can bring in an image and preview it, or I can ask AI to generate a background and preview those options. Once happy with the result, I can save out these images and use them anywhere. ## AI Activation and Pattern Management From 2025.1 and onward, by default, all AI features will be deactivated. If you wish to use AI, you will need to activate it manually. For individual users, this can be found through your My Page. For enterprise users, this can be found through your account page. You will now have the option to save out selected patterns and trims as a garment, making it easier to take separate parts of a project file and add them into other project files. For instance, here, I would like to add this crossbody bag into another project file I have. Now, with this feature, I can easily do this and create a complete outfit quickly. ## Zipper Tab and Object Browser Enhancements We have added a zipper tab within our object browser, allowing you to now save out a trim as a whole option and also apply trims quickly and easily within your workspace. You will be able to edit and adjust parts of the zipper individually while also editing it as a whole, all within the property editor. We have combined the fabric creator with our seamless texture generator to become one CloLab. This will also connect to our new ZFAB kit, available for pre-order now. Within CloLab, you can create your fabric information at the very top and then go into our map section and bring in your PBR maps. Using the same process as our seamless texture generator, you can then start to create a seamless repeat, either using Clo's help or manually. Once you have the repeat you like, you can then move into the physical properties and follow the same process as the fabric creator. Add in the fabric type, composition, and weight, and then see the drape change in real-time. Once happy with your fabric physics and visuals, you can then save this out as one ZFAB with all the textures and physical properties combined. This can then be brought into your object browser and applied to your garment. ## Colorway Management and Grading Now, when adding a project or garment, you will be able to choose which colorways to add. If there are fewer colorways in the current file, Clo will simply add the first colorway to the remaining, allowing you to add and adjust the additional colorways. Grading within Clo has never been easier. Now, within Clo, you can choose which points should or shouldn't be graded. Through the right-click option, you can either convert to a non-graded point or a graded point. If the point becomes non-graded, it will follow the grading rules of the graded point closest to it. This will also apply to curve points. We hope this makes grading easier for everyone within Clo. ## Plotter Snapshot Options Within 2025.1, we have updated our plotter snapshot options further, adding in the ability to color code the lines along with applying different line styles. We hope this will increase the usability of the plotter files themselves to more than just printing and maybe even cutting machines, making production with Clo more achievable. ## DXF Import/Export Now within Clo, you can export and import standard DXFs, allowing for more DXF options and more interoperability within other CAD software. Within the DXF export or import popup in the dropdown menu, there will now be a DXF option. This will be for standard or classic DXF files. ## AI Pattern Drafting Our pattern drafter has expanded with its AI capabilities to now be able to read any image, not just a sketch outline. Now you can drop in a picture of a garment you like, and the pattern drafter will draft a pattern from that image alone. As you can see here, you can keep editing it around using the measurements. Once happy, you can select "Create," and then the garment will automatically be arranged and sewn on the avatar for you. ## 2D CAD Tool Improvements A really nice improvement we have made to our 2D CAD tools is the ability to now extend to the half-symmetric line on half-symmetrical patterns, making it so you no longer have to deal with duplicate internal lines, making editing internal lines even easier.

I can hit **Save**, and then all of these lights will save together, allowing me to bring them into other project files. I can hit **Open**, and it will come in here. You may not see the difference because this is already set up, but you know, I can just start and play. ## Conclusion And that's all! Thanks so much for watching. summary: ```markdown # Sewing Relationships in Bomber Jacket Design In this video, Sam from @Sam_Fromonline explores the concept of sewing relationships while constructing a bomber jacket pattern. ## Understanding Sewing Relationships So, these colored lines that are connecting all of my pattern pieces are called threads and represent sewing relationships. Today, we're going to take a look at how many sewing relationships it takes to construct this bomber jacket pattern that I designed. ## Constructing the Bomber Jacket ### Initial Structure Starting with one sewing relationship, I'm adding the shoulders and side seams, which makes for four sewing relationships. This creates a kind of vest shape. ### Adding Sleeves Now, we're adding two two-part sleeves to the vest shape. This brings the total to 17 sewing relationships. ### Expanding the Design We jumped up a few numbers with this next addition, incorporating cuffs, ribbing, and a collar, which results in 46 unique sewing relationships. At this stage, the jacket is basically finished, minus a few pockets. ## Final Touches After adding two double-layered front flap pockets, a sleeve pocket, and a zipper facing, we completed the jacket with 77 unique sewing relationships. ## Conclusion Honestly, I really love looking at the pattern diagram with all the sewing lines going everywhere. It looks like such a mess, but also so technical and symmetric at the same time. transcript:
Hello, this is a connect team. In CAP
tutorial 1, we introduced how to create
a cap using the cap mold and visor from
connect. In this video, we'll take it a
step further by sharing practical tips
that can be applied in your production
process. Let's start by loading the cap
asset. Open the CL library and go to the
garment category and navigate to the
connect asset tab. In the search bar,
type midprofile. You'll now see both
male and female cap assets in the
library window. These assets feature a
standard six panel cap design with a
fully constructed snapback. They're
built using the mid-profile cap mold and
halfcurved visor. So, if you want to
match the same silhouette, make sure to
use the same mold and visor types. Now,
let's doubleclick on the male version to
load it into the workspace. Next, let's
load the cap mold and visor. Go to the
avatar tab in the CL library. Navigate
asset tab. Search for mid-profile mold
and half curved visor. Load each item
into the CL. When loading these files,
make sure to click the add option. If
you don't, the current avatar will be
replaced and your existing work may be
lost. Once the visor is loaded, adjust
its angle to align properly with the
cap.
Then select both the mold and visor and
set their skin offset to zero.
Now let's move on to creating the
details of the cap. We'll start by
adding a bias tape. Since the process of
creating and attaching bias tape was
covered in detail in tutorial 1, we'll
go through this step quickly. If you'd
like a more in-depth explanation, please
refer to the tutorial one video.
Next, let's create the back opening bias
tape. This process is also covered in
tutorial 1, but in this video, we'll
take you from understanding the process
to applying it in practice.
For designs with a back opening such as
this asset, the bias tape will be rolled
and sewn together with the seam
allowance when making the actual
construction. In this case, the outline
length of the back opening with seam
allowance will be shorter than the
outline length of the pattern without
seam allowance.
Then, when the seam is rolled with bias
tape, the final length of the back
opening ends up being the same as the
length of the seam outline. This process
gives the back opening a neat rounded
shape. However, since CL uses patterns
without seam allowance by default, it's
difficult to simulate the rolled sewing
process accurately.
So, in this video, we'll walk you
through how to predict the final length
of the back opening and create the bias
tape accordingly.
A method that closely resembles the
actual production process. First, let's
create a seam just like in the real
production.
Right click on the back opening segment
and select extend pattern outline. Then
a dialogue window will appear. In this
case, we'll input 0.25 in for the seam
width.
Now that the seam allowance has been
created, click on its outer edge to
check the outline length. You can check
the length at this point. Next, let's
create a bias tape pattern based on that
length. Select the rectangle tool. Click
on an empty area in the 2D pattern
window and enter the dimensions in the
dialogue window.
Set the width to the outline length you
just measured and the height to the seam
width which is 0.25 in.
Once the bias tape is created, we'll
need it on both sides. Right click on
the center line and select unfold
symmetric editing with sewing.
Now we no longer need the seam allowance
pattern we created earlier. Use the
trace tool. Right click on the baseline
and select cut to remove it.
Finally, let's create an internal line
where the bias tape will be sewn. Right
click on the back opening outline again
and select offset as internal line. In
the dialogue window, enter 0.25 in which
is the width of the bias tape and click
okay. Now let's move on to sewing the
bias tape. Before we do that, let's
understand how this process works in
actual production. In actual sewing,
when bias tape is applied along a curved
area, it tends to follow the shorter
seam line, which causes the final length
to shrink slightly. On the other hand,
for straight areas, such as the bottom
edge, there's little to no change in
length even after the tape is sewn.
Also, in areas where the bias tape is
sewn in multiple layers, the fabric
becomes thickly stacked.
As a result, there is little to no
change in length. Therefore, in clo as
well, we will sew the bias tape at a 1x1
ratio along the straight bottom edge and
in the layered section where the tape is
attached.
Now, let's use the free sewing tool to
sew the bias tape to the back opening.
Start by clicking and dragging along the
back opening from the bottom edge up to
the point where the curve begins. If
you're unsure how much of the section to
select, simply sew up to the height of
the snap as a reference.
After clicking the starting point, right
click and enter the desired length in
the dialogue window.
Repeat the same click and drag action on
the bias tape pattern and finish sewing
by clicking at the snap point. For the
remaining parts, also sew with a 1x one
length ratio. Next, sew the upper part
in the same way with a 1x one ratio.
Then, select the remaining portion and
complete the rest of the sewing.
Change the sewing line type to turned.
Before running the simulation, select
the pattern and lower the particle
distance to five and set the collision
thickness to zero. To arrange the
pattern, right click on the tape pattern
in the 3D window and select superimpose
under. You'll see the pattern placed
along the sewing line. Finally, apply
strengthen to the entire pattern and run
the simulation.
Now, let's create the sweatb band and
add some realistic detailing. In
tutorial 1, we already covered how to
create a basic one- layer sweatb band
similar to an elastic band. So, in this
video, we'll focus on making a more
realistic double layer quilted
sweatband.
By constructing the pattern with two
layers, we can simulate a more
substantial and detailed thickness just
like the real thing. Right click on the
top edge of the sweatb band and click
offset pattern outline. Set the distance
to 1 in and make sure to check create
internal line so that an internal line
is automatically generated as the
pattern extends. This line will be used
later for folding. You'll now see the
extended pattern appear in the 3D
window. From the 3D toolbar, select the
fold arrangement tool and click on the
internal line at the center. You'll see
red and green gizmos appear. Click and
drag the appropriate gizmo to fold the
pattern in half.
Before running the simulation, sew the
top and bottom outlines together and
change the sewing line type to turned.
Then double check that the particle
distance is set to five and the
collision thickness is zero. Now run the
simulation. Once the simulation is
complete, let's add stitch lines to
simulate the quilted finish. Right click
on the center line of the pattern and
select offset as internal line. In the
dialogue box, set the number of offsets
to two and the distance to 0.33 in.
To apply the lines on both sides of the
center, check both sides, then click
okay. This will generate two evenly
spaced internal lines at 0.33 in
intervals, perfect for quilting detail.
Once the internal lines have been
created, sew each line and run the
simulation.
The number of quilting lines may vary
depending on the design.
If the simulation becomes unstable due
to overlapping pattern layers, use the
gizmo to slightly move the visor pattern
forward. This will help prevent
collision between patterns and ensure a
stable simulation.
Next, let's add detailing to the visor.
In actual hat construction, the visor
typically consists of two layers of
fabric that wrap around a visor pad. To
recreate this in clo, we'll use the
layer clone feature to create a double
layered visor. Before that, let's add
the stitching lines to the visor. When
you use layer clone on a pattern with
internal lines, CL automatically
duplicates the pattern and stitches it
along those lines. So, it's best to add
the stitching lines first. Right click
on the outer edge of the visor pattern
and select offset as internal line. In
the dialogue window, set the number of
offsets to five to create five stitching
lines. Then switch the distance option
to individual to define each offset
separately. For the first internal line,
enter 0.5 in as it should sit slightly
inward from the edge. For the remaining
lines, enter 0.25 in for each to evenly
space them out. Once you've completed
the setup, click okay to generate the
internal lines. Now, let's create a
double layered visor to replicate the
real construction where the visor pad is
sandwiched between two fabric layers.
Right click on the visor pattern and
click layer clone under. Then click on
an empty space in the 2D window to place
the cloned pattern. You'll see that the
internal lines are automatically sewn
together with the new layer. To simulate
the visor pad thickness, select the top
pattern and apply an additional
thickness of three in the property
editor.
Adjust the curvature to 20% to give the
edge a more angular appearance.
By default, the additional thickness
collision is set to zero. This can cause
the top layer to sink into the bottom
layer during simulation.
So, increase the additional thickness
collision to three and use superimpose
under to correctly place the bottom
layer.
To maintain the shape of both layers,
select the visor patterns, right click,
and apply solidify.
Make sure freeze is unchecked.
Set strengthen to 80 for a firmer
structure and run the simulation.
You'll see the visor hold its form more
accurately.
Next, let's apply Solidify to the crown
pieces. In real hats, the front crown
panels are reinforced with a stiff
interlining to maintain the hat's
profile.
Reflecting this, apply Solidify 100 to
the front crown panel. For the remaining
crown panels, apply a solidify value of
40 to simulate a softer structure.
Run the simulation and check the overall
shape.
If any sewing lines have come undone,
especially on the snap pattern where
seam allowances were previously created
and cut, make sure to reso them to
prevent the patterns from detaching.
When looking at the visor, you'll notice
that the thickness direction is
currently set to both, causing the visor
pattern to extend above the crown
pattern. In this case, if you change the
extrusion direction to backward, the
thickness surface will be directed
downward. In this case, the lower
pattern may become hidden due to the
overlapping thickness. To resolve this,
you can reposition it using the
superimpose under function. However,
since the upper pattern's thickness now
extends downward, you must assign a
sufficient collision value to prevent
the two patterns from overlapping. To
ensure proper placement, it is
recommended to set the collision
thickness of the lower pattern to three,
matching the thickness of the upper
pattern. If you want to add more
thickness to the lower pattern, increase
the value in the additional thickness
rendering.
Next, let's add details such as applying
fabric, the top stitching, and the top
button. These steps are also explained
in tutorial one. So, we'll go through
them quickly in this video.
Finally, let's import a different type
of visor and make changes to it. Connect
offers various types of visors and in
this case we'll work with curved one.
Doubleclick the asset to import it
and delete the halfcurved visor that was
previously imported.
Now adjust the angle of the newly loaded
visor to the desired angle and change
the skin offset to zero.
Now to ensure smooth simulation, please
delete the lower pattern and remove the
sewing lines with the crown patterns.
Select all crown patterns and freeze
them.
At the same time, unfreeze and
unsolidify the visor.
Apply strengthen to the visor and run
the simulation. You'll see the pattern
naturally simulate to the visor's
curvature.
To simulate a perfect fit to the visor
shape, we apply a negative pressure
value.
Once the pattern simulates the visor,
stop the simulation and apply solidify
again. Now reso the patterns and adjust
the fold angle accordingly.
And don't forget to reset the pressure
back to zero. Let's unstrengthen the
visor pattern for better stability
during simulation. Slightly adjust the
position of the pattern and visor to
place them as close to the crown as
possible.
Now simulate again. Your curved visor is
complete.
We've covered several methods for
accurately constructing cap reflecting
real production processes.
Now try designing your own styles using
the various molds and visor types
available in connect.

Right-click on the back opening outline again and select "Offset as Internal Line." In the dialogue window, enter 0.25 in, which is the width of the bias tape, and click "OK." ## Sewing the Bias Tape Now let's move on to sewing the bias tape. Before we do that, let's understand how this process works in actual production. In actual sewing, when bias tape is applied along a curved area, it tends to follow the shorter seam line, which causes the final length to shrink slightly. On the other hand, for straight areas, such as the bottom edge, there's little to no change in length even after the tape is sewn. Also, in areas where the bias tape is sewn in multiple layers, the fabric becomes thickly stacked. As a result, there is little to no change in length. The number of quilting lines may vary depending on the design. If the simulation becomes unstable due to overlapping pattern layers, use the gizmo to slightly move the visor pattern forward. This will help prevent collision between patterns and ensure a stable simulation. ## Detailing the Visor Next, let's add detailing to the visor. In actual hat construction, the visor typically consists of two layers of fabric that wrap around a visor pad. To recreate this in CLO, we'll use the layer clone feature to create a double-layered visor. Before that, let's add the stitching lines to the visor. ### Adding Stitching Lines When you use layer clone on a pattern with internal lines, CL automatically duplicates the pattern and stitches it along those lines. In the dialogue window, set the number of offsets to five to create five stitching lines. Then switch the distance option to "Individual" to define each offset separately. For the first internal line, enter 0.5 in as it should sit slightly inward from the edge. For the remaining lines, enter 0.25 in for each to evenly space them out. Once you've completed the setup, click "OK" to generate the internal lines. ### Creating a Double-Layered Visor Now, let's create a double-layered visor to replicate the real construction where the visor pad is sandwiched between two fabric layers. summary: ```markdown # Cap Tutorial 1: Creating Caps Using the Cap Mold ## Introduction Hello, this is the Connect team. I’d like to introduce how to create hats using the newly released cap molds and visors. ## Cap Mold and Visor Overview A cap mold refers to the base form that defines the overall shape of a hat, while a visor refers to the mold used to create the brim at the front. These two components are key elements that determine the design of a hat. The newly released cap molds and visors are available in both men's and women's versions and support a variety of design styles. ### Profiles and Types For the cap molds, three different profiles are provided for men and women respectively. For the visors, a total of four types are available, allowing for various brim curvatures. You can find the download links for the cap molds and visors in the description. ## Getting Started Now, let's learn how to make a hat using these newly released cap molds and visors. You can click the link in the description to download the assets for this tutorial from the Connect official store. ### Tools and Materials In this video, we'll be using the commonly used middle profile mold and a half-curved visor. Once you've downloaded them, let’s import the middle profile mold into Claw. ## Importing the Mold When you import the mold, you'll notice the ear dummy. We'll be designing the hat to sit above the ears so that it doesn't pass through the ear dummy. If you're working on a design that covers the ears, right-click above the ear dummy and select deactivate avatar to disable it. Then in the property editor, set the opacity to zero to proceed with the creation. ## Drawing Guidelines The mold files provided by Connect come with pre-drawn guidelines to make designing easier. You can either use these lines as they are or draw your own if needed. In this video, we'll start by showing you how to draw simple guidelines. ### Activating Guidelines First, activate the "Show 3D Pen" and "Show Avatar Measure" icons from the avatar display menu at the top left. This will display all the guidelines needed for hat making. Among these, we'll delete the circumference guideline and redraw it. 1. From the 3D toolbar, select the "Edit Measure" tool. Click on the purple line and press delete. 2. Next, select the "Edit 3D Pen" tool. Double-click on the black line to select all of it and press delete. 3. Then select the "3D Avatar Pen" tool located under the "Edit 3D Pen" tool and click a point above the ear dummy. While holding shift, right-click and drag to rotate the view as you place points around the head. 4. Continue placing points and finally return to the first point to complete the line. This line will serve as a guide for creating the hat pattern. ## Measuring and Drawing Additional Guidelines Next, we're going to draw a measuring tape to ensure stable hat pattern construction. 1. On the 3D toolbar, select the "Basic Circumference Measure" tool. To use this tool, start by clicking once above the ear dummy, then hold shift and click two more times horizontally. This will create the circumference measuring tape. 2. Now, to create a complete crown pattern, we'll finish drawing the remaining design lines. Select the "3D Avatar Pen" tool. Then press the number five on your keyboard to switch to the top view. You'll see a measure tape drawn along the center of the mold. Follow this tape and draw a line using the 3D pen. 3. Then draw additional lines to divide the crown into three equal sections based on the center line. ## Generating the Pattern Now let's generate the pattern from the design lines drawn with a 3D Avatar Pen. 1. Press and hold the "3D Avatar Pen" tool. Then select the "Flatten" function. 2. Click on all the surfaces divided by the design lines and press enter on your keyboard. You'll see that patterns are created in both 3D and 2D views following the selected shapes. ### Adjusting the Pattern Now let's adjust the generated pattern to the desired shape. 1. First, in the 2D pattern window, use the "Transform Pattern" tool to neatly align the patterns in order. 2. Then select the "Edit Style Line" tool from the 3D toolbar to make modifications directly in 3D. When you select a pattern, you'll notice its outline highlighted with a bold solid line. 3. Click and drag the segment you want to modify, and you'll see that the sewn patterns connected to it will adjust accordingly as well. Once you've roughly shaped the pattern in 3D, let's fine-tune it in 2D for more precise detailing. If there are any unnecessary segment points, use the "Edit Pattern" tool from the 2D toolbar, right-click, and select "Convert to Curve Point." Then choose "Maintain Curve" to turn them into curve points. Next, hold down the "Edit Pattern" tool to switch to the "Edit Curve Point" tool. Remove any extra curve points and adjust the pattern's curves to get the shape you want. ## Securing and Finalizing the Pattern Once the pattern modifications are complete, click the "Transform Pattern" tool in the 2D toolbar and select all patterns in the 2D window. 1. Right-click on the pattern and choose "Symmetric Pattern with Sewing" to duplicate the pattern symmetrically. 2. After duplicating, use the "Segment Sewing Tool" to sew the center front and back where the sewing lines haven't been set yet. Once the patterns have been symmetrically copied, let's adjust a few settings to ensure smooth simulation. 1. First, select the mold and set the skin offset to zero in the property editor window. 2. Next, select all the crown patterns and set the particle distance to five and the thickness collision to one in the property editor. 3. Finally, for a stable simulation, right-click on the patterns and choose "Strengthen" before running the simulation. Strengthen temporarily makes the selected pattern stiffer, helping them maintain their shape during simulation. ## Creating the Back Opening Next, we'll create the back opening on the back of the hat using the internal line tool. While drawing the back opening line, hold down the control key to create it as a curve. After drawing the line, use the "Edit Curve Point" tool to refine it into the desired shape. Once the line is finalized, select the internal line with the "Edit Pattern" tool, right-click, and choose "Cut." Delete the cutout pattern piece afterward. Once the back opening is complete, let's secure the patterns to the mold before working on the inside of the hat. Press and hold the "Edit Measure" tool in the 3D toolbar and select the "Attach to Measure" tool. Click the bottom line of each crown pattern. Then click the measure tape that was created above the ear. After attaching all patterns to the measure tape, run the simulation. You'll see that the patterns are now fixed along the measure tape line. ## Creating the Bias Tape Now we're going to create the bias tape that goes inside the hat. Before making the bias tape pattern, we need to check the tape length by creating an internal line. The bias tape width will be set to 0.5 inches. 1. Select the outline of the crown pattern. Right-click and choose "Offset as Internal Line" to create an internal line at 0.25 inches. 2. Do the same for the rest of the outlines by creating internal lines with the same width. When selecting two segments at the same time, the lines won't intersect; instead, they'll connect at the crossing points. So, make sure to select each outline individually to create the internal lines. Once all the outlines have internal lines, check in the 3D garment window to see if each internal segment is properly connected and adjust them so they meet correctly. ### Adding Internal Lines for Sewing To sew the tape, you'll also need to add additional internal lines between the existing ones to connect them. Since the patterns are symmetric, creating them on one side will automatically generate them on the mirrored side as well. Now, let's check the length of the bias tape by clicking on the internal lines. 1. First, we'll measure the bias tape that connects the front and back panel patterns. 2. Select the "Edit Pattern" tool. Hold shift and select all the segments that need to be sewn. 3. Then, check the length in the property editor window. ## Creating the Bias Tape Pattern Now let's create the bias tape pattern using the rectangle tool. 1. After selecting the tool, click on the 2D pattern window and a dialogue box will appear. Enter 0.5 inches for the width and 11.82 inches for the height to create the pattern. 2. Use the same method to check the length of the side bias tape and create the corresponding pattern. If you're unsure about where the tape connects, hold shift and select multiple patterns in the 3D garment window to check their positions. You'll see the corresponding picking points highlighted in the 2D pattern window. Since the side bias tapes are identical on both sides, you only need to make one, sew it, and then copy it as a symmetric pattern. ### Adding Stitch Lines Before sewing the bias tape patterns to the crown, let's add stitch lines to enhance the detail. Assuming the stitch offset is 1/16th inch, select all the long outer segments of the two bias tape patterns, right-click, and choose "Offset as Internal Line" to create an internal line 0.063

summary: ```markdown # Grading Improvements | Clo 2025.0 Features Deep Dive ## Introduction Hey everyone, my name is Phoebe, and we have some great updates for you regarding grading. So, let's jump in and have some fun while we learn! ## Grading Tools Overview All of our grading tools are located in your 2D toolbar off to the side at the very bottom. If you can't find them, you might want to look right here. You'll see little lines underneath the sewing tool or something similar. You can move and pop it out to view more of your tools. If you're working on a smaller screen, it may be far down, and you might only see this tool. You can click and hold down on the two black lines to move it out. ### Edit Grading Tool What this tool will do is allow you to edit your grading. You can select a line and add in some grading in multiple ways. You can click here and use the arrow keys to control your movement. That will be down below. So, you can decide how much you want to adjust with each arrow stroke. For example, clicking out adjusts by 0.25 every time. ### Measurement Adjustments One of our nice updates is that you can also go down into your measurements here and, using your arrow keys, increase or decrease by 1 to change these around. After making your adjustments, you can hit enter, and it will change. For instance, I just changed the medium size by two. You can always go back to zero, hit enter, and change it down. This functionality allows you to change all measurements easily using your arrow keys. ## Individual Measurement Editing There’s the Edit Each Measurement tool located below the Edit Curve Grading tool. This allows you to edit each size individually. After selecting it, you will see all of your curve points and be able to edit those as needed. You can also edit each graded size curve by clicking and moving each graded size curve point if necessary. ### Grading Table Functionality Within the grading table, you can show and hide information. You can also export this box, allowing it to pop out for a reformatted view of how it looks. You will see distance and offset, which may make it easier for you to edit your grading and adjust it horizontally. The offsets are purposefully placed between graded sizes to indicate the difference between sizes, such as small to medium. You can double-click to increase or change it. For example, if you want to set it to one, you can change it to two or revert back to zero. You can adjust all offsets simultaneously or individually as needed. ## Avatar Size Pairing Another update involves the avatar feature. I have small, medium, large, and extra-large avatars paired with these sizes. For example, if I check on my avatar for medium, I can see that the avatar for medium corresponds correctly. This feature allows you to see which avatar is being used for each graded size, making life a lot easier. ## Graphic Grading Updates Finally, we have updates regarding grading for graphics. I already have some grading in place, and now we can use percentages for grading. You can switch to percentage or unit measurements. Additionally, you can lock your aspect ratio to ensure that your graphic maintains its proportions. For instance, if I set medium to 100 and large to 100, I can then adjust large to 115, and it will automatically adjust the height and width to keep that aspect ratio intact. This functionality is beneficial for maintaining consistent sizing across graphics. ## Conclusion These are just some of our updates to grading. We hope we've made it a lot easier for you! Thanks so much for watching. If you have any questions, please use the comment section down below. Don’t forget to like and subscribe, and check out all of the great videos we have on our YouTube channel. There is so much valuable information there. summary: ```markdown # Plotter Improvements For Pattern Printing | Clo 2025.0 Features Deep Dive Hey everyone, my name is Phoebe and we have some great updates with our print layout and exporting to Plotter. So, let's dive on in and have some fun while we learn. ## Setting Up Your Pattern Okay, so I have my pattern all set up. I've nested it, and I've added in seam allowance. I am ready to export this out to my plotter. I've even got some annotations in there. ## Exporting to the Plotter There are a few ways in which you can export out to a plotter. I'm going to go through two ways in which we've updated. ### Snapshot Method The first way is to use the little snapshot icon right here. You can select it inside of your print layout, which you can access through your modes. Go to print layout here, and in your print layout toolbar, all the way at the bottom, there's a snapshot option. 1. **Select Snapshot**: I can select this, read a snapshot, and one of the nice updates we've done is you can uncheck pattern outlines if you'd like, so that only your seam allowance is being shown, which is really, really helpful. 2. **Customize Your View**: You can uncheck various elements: - Pattern outlines - Base lines - Internal lines - Graphic lines - Reference lines - Symmetrical instance lines Maybe you just want seam allowance and internal lines, or perhaps you just want seam allowance and pattern outlines. It’s whatever you'd like. 3. **Additional Information**: You also can then show additional information or uncheck it all. We’ve also added nesting header information to the bottom, which you can use as well, along with pattern names and pattern annotations. 4. **Choose Your Format**: After customizing, you can choose your format that you'd like. I'm going to do one, and you can then save, and that will all be saved out. ### File Export Method Another way is to go to the top toolbar, select File, and then choose Export to Plotter. This pop-up window will come up, and again, we have separated out notches and baselines. 1. **Customize Your Export**: - Keep your notches, and maybe you want to uncheck baselines. - You might also not want graphic lines or reference lines. - If you want pattern outlines, you can choose to have dotted or dashed lines. You won't see it here, but you should see it when you export it and save it. 2. **Size Options**: You also have the ability to either shrink to fit or use actual size. I’m going to shrink to fit so that it all shrinks into my pattern and nothing goes outside of it. 3. **Final Adjustments**: I'm going to keep this dotted. Then I can save, and you can see all right here how that looks along with all of that information. It might be a little blurry right now, but you can see the dash lines here, your notches, the seam allowance, and all of that. ### Conclusion All saved and viewable in your water file. Pretty cool, right? Thanks so much for watching! If you have any questions, use that comment section down below, and one of our CLO designers will get back to you. Don't forget to check out all the other great videos we have on our YouTube channel. Thanks again so much for watching, and keep having fun in CLO! ```
